def combine(
    self,
    on: str | Sequence[str] | None = None,
    *,
    how: str = "full",
    allow_common_columns: bool = True,
) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Combine all dataframes into one.

    With no arguments, this method preserves the legacy behavior exactly: it
    merges all DataFrames by performing a full join on every column they share,
    not only ``ID``. A row whose shared columns hold nulls matches nothing, so it
    appears twice: once from each side. This happens, for example, when BQL has
    no ``DATE`` for a security in two items. If no common columns are found, it
    raises a ValueError.

    Use ``combine(on="ID")`` for one row per security. When ``on`` is provided,
    only those columns are used as join keys. Other overlapping columns are
    preserved with a suffix unless ``allow_common_columns`` is false.

    Args:
        on: Explicit column or columns to join on. If omitted, legacy common-column
            joining is used.
        how: Polars join strategy to use when ``on`` is provided.
        allow_common_columns: Whether overlapping non-key columns are allowed when
            ``on`` is provided. If true, right-hand overlapping columns are suffixed
            with the corresponding BQL item name.

    Returns:
        pl.DataFrame: Combined dataframe.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If no dataframes are present (the message includes the BQL
            error, if any), if no common columns exist in legacy mode, if
            explicit join keys are missing, or if overlapping non-key columns
            are disallowed.

    Example:
        One row per security; the ``DATE`` of the second item gets a suffix:

        ```python
        from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

        with BQuery() as bq:
            result = bq.bql(
                "get(px_last, px_volume) "
                "for(['IBM US Equity', 'NOT A SECURITY Equity'])"
            )
        print(result.combine(on="ID"))
        ```

        Expected output:
        ```python
        shape: (2, 6)
        ┌───────────────────────┬─────────┬────────────┬──────────┬───────────┬────────────────┐
        │ ID                    ┆ px_last ┆ DATE       ┆ CURRENCY ┆ px_volume ┆ DATE_px_volume │
        │ ---                   ┆ ---     ┆ ---        ┆ ---      ┆ ---       ┆ ---            │
        │ str                   ┆ f64     ┆ date       ┆ str      ┆ f64       ┆ date           │
        ╞═══════════════════════╪═════════╪════════════╪══════════╪═══════════╪════════════════╡
        │ IBM US Equity         ┆ 247.13  ┆ 2026-11-16 ┆ USD      ┆ 4750.0    ┆ 2026-11-16     │
        │ NOT A SECURITY Equity ┆ null    ┆ null       ┆ null     ┆ null      ┆ null           │
        └───────────────────────┴─────────┴────────────┴──────────┴───────────┴────────────────┘
        ```

        Without ``on``, the join uses ``ID`` and ``DATE``; the security without
        a ``DATE`` appears twice:

        ```python
        print(result.combine())
        ```

        Expected output:
        ```python
        shape: (3, 5)
        ┌───────────────────────┬─────────┬────────────┬──────────┬───────────┐
        │ ID                    ┆ px_last ┆ DATE       ┆ CURRENCY ┆ px_volume │
        │ ---                   ┆ ---     ┆ ---        ┆ ---      ┆ ---       │
        │ str                   ┆ f64     ┆ date       ┆ str      ┆ f64       │
        ╞═══════════════════════╪═════════╪════════════╪══════════╪═══════════╡
        │ IBM US Equity         ┆ 247.13  ┆ 2026-11-16 ┆ USD      ┆ 4750.0    │
        │ NOT A SECURITY Equity ┆ null    ┆ null       ┆ null     ┆ null      │
        │ NOT A SECURITY Equity ┆ null    ┆ null       ┆ null     ┆ null      │
        └───────────────────────┴─────────┴────────────┴──────────┴───────────┘
        ```

    """  # noqa: E501
    if not self.dataframes:
        if self.errors:
            raise ValueError(
                "No DataFrames to combine. BQL error: " + "; ".join(self.errors)
            )
        raise ValueError("No DataFrames to combine.")

    if on is not None:
        return self._combine_on(
            on, how=how, allow_common_columns=allow_common_columns
        )

    # Legacy mode, kept as it always was: join on every column the frames share.
    if how != "full":
        raise ValueError("The 'how' parameter requires explicit join keys via 'on'.")
    if not allow_common_columns:
        raise ValueError(
            "The 'allow_common_columns' parameter requires explicit join keys "
            "via 'on'."
        )

    result = self.dataframes[0]
    for df in self.dataframes[1:]:
        common_cols = [col for col in result.columns if col in df.columns]
        if not common_cols:
            raise ValueError("No common columns found to join on.")
        result = result.join(df, on=common_cols, how="full", coalesce=True)
    return result

docs.title: Developer guide
docs.text:
You have a bug report or a feature idea for polars-bloomberg. Three facts keep the work small:

  • The code is one file. Almost everything is in polars_bloomberg/plbbg.py, and it reads from top to bottom.
  • Every call runs the same five steps. When you can read bdp, you can read the other four methods.
  • You need no Bloomberg Terminal. The tests replay recorded Bloomberg answers, and a user's failing call can be saved to a file and replayed on your machine.

The first six sections, up to Find where a bug is, are a tour: read them in order, in about eight minutes. The sections after them are for looking things up.

You want to Go to run the tests for the first time Set up find the code behind a wrong result Find where a bug is reproduce a user's bug without a Terminal Capture a failing case know whether a strange behavior is Bloomberg's Bloomberg quirks the code handles add an option or a new method Add an option, Add a new request type know what a pull request must satisfy Before you open a pull request

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
In your clone of the repository:

uv sync --extra dev --extra docs
uv run pytest

All tests pass in about a second. The live tests are reported as skipped: they run only with pytest --bbg, at a Bloomberg Terminal.

The other commands on this page are written without uv run. Put it in front of each, or activate the environment once: source .venv/bin/activate, on Windows .venv\Scripts\activate.

blpapi is not on PyPI; pyproject.toml tells uv where Bloomberg publishes it. Without uv, run pip install -r requirements.txt and then pip install -e ".[dev]" in an environment of your own.

docs.title: The library in one minute
docs.text:
polars-bloomberg is five methods on BQuery: bdp, bdh, bdib, bql and bsrch. Each one sends one Bloomberg request and turns the answer into one Polars DataFrame (bql returns a BqlResult, which holds one DataFrame per item of the query).

Every method runs the same five steps. This is bdp without its docstring:

def bdp(self, securities, fields, overrides=None, options=None):
    # Step 1: check the inputs.
    securities = _as_list(securities)
    fields = _as_list(fields)
    _check_no_field_is_named(fields, "security")

    # Step 2: build the request.
    request = self._create_request("//blp/refdata", "ReferenceDataRequest")
    _append_values(request, "securities", securities)
    _append_values(request, "fields", fields)
    _set_overrides(request, overrides)
    _set_options(request, options)

    # Steps 3 to 5: send it, parse the answer, build the DataFrame.
    payloads = self._send_request(request)
    rows = _parse_bdp(payloads, fields)
    schema = {"security": pl.String, **dict.fromkeys(fields)}
    return pl.DataFrame(rows, schema=schema, infer_schema_length=None)

A payload is one message of Bloomberg's answer as plain Python (msg.toPy()): dicts, lists, numbers, strings and dates. The schema names the columns and gives a dtype to security only; Polars infers the dtype of each field from all rows.

Only step 3 talks to Bloomberg, and it does so through one object, the session:

bq.bdp(...)                                                         DataFrame
    │                                                                   ▲
    ▼                                                                   │
1 check inputs ─► 2 build request ─► 3 send ─► 4 parse answer ─► 5 build DataFrame
                                      │  ▲
                              request ▼  │ payloads
                                   the session
                      live:   Bloomberg answers
                      tests:  a fake session replays a recorded answer

This is why the offline tests need no Bloomberg. They call the public methods on a BQuery whose session is a FakeSession (in tests/support.py). All five steps run as they do for a user; only the answer comes from a file.

The other four methods read the same way. They differ in these places:

Method Service Request Parser What is different bdp //blp/refdata ReferenceDataRequest _parse_bdp the model for the others bdh //blp/refdata HistoricalDataRequest _parse_bdh two dates in the request; one security per payload bdib //blp/refdata IntradayBarRequest _parse_bdib one security; times instead of dates, in UTC; fixed columns bql //blp/bqlsvc sendQuery _parse_bql the answer is JSON text; one DataFrame per item; errors are part of the answer bsrch //blp/exrsvc ExcelGetGridRequest _parse_bsrch overrides are sent as text; the answer is a grid without column types

docs.title: Words used on this page
docs.text:
The first seven rows are Bloomberg's words, which you will also meet in Bloomberg's documentation. The last four belong to this repository.

Word Meaning security, field What a request asks about (IBM US Equity) and what it asks for (PX_LAST). override A value that replaces one that Bloomberg would otherwise use in a calculation, for example REFERENCE_DATE. option A setting of the request itself, for example periodicitySelection. session The connection to Bloomberg, a blpapi.Session. BQuery.start() opens it. service A group of request types, for example //blp/refdata. A session opens a service before it uses it. event, message Bloomberg answers in events, and an event holds messages. The last event of an answer has the type RESPONSE; the events before it have the type PARTIAL_RESPONSE. correlation ID The ticket that the session returns when a request is sent. Every message of the answer carries it. payload One message as plain Python. debug dump The JSON file that BQuery(debug=True) writes for each request: the request and the messages that came back. recording A debug dump stored in tests/data/recordings/, with the result of the call added as "expected". scenario A named call in tests/recordings.py. Its answer is the recording of the same name.

Each section starts with a banner comment, so a search for # 3. takes you to section 3. The table names the main functions of each section.

Inputs and requests _as_list, _check_no_field_is_named, _yyyymmdd, _append_values, _set_overrides, _override_pairs, _set_options an input is refused or sent in the wrong form 3. bdp and bdh _parse_bdp, _parse_bdh, _security_errors, _warn_security_errors a value or row is missing; a warning about a security or field is wrong 4. bdib _iso_datetime, _BAR_SCHEMA, _parse_bdib times are off; a bar column is missing 5. bql _set_bql_client_context, _parse_bql, _load_bql_answers, _bql_item, _BQL_DTYPES, _bql_number, _bql_date, _bql_datetime, _bql_dataframe a BQL column has the wrong type or name; an error message is lost 6. bsrch _set_bsrch_overrides, _parse_bsrch, _cell_value, _blank_strings_to_none a search column has the wrong type or title 7. BqlResult the frames of a BQL answer and combine() joining BQL items gives unexpected rows or columns 8. Debug dump _write_debug_dump, _json_default you change what BQuery(debug=True) writes

docs.title: One call, end to end
docs.text:
Take bq.bdp(["IBM US Equity", "NOT A SECURITY Equity"], ["NAME"]): one security that exists and one that does not. Bloomberg's answer to it is stored in tests/data/recordings/bdp/invalid_security_mixed.json.

  1. Check the inputs. _as_list lets a caller pass one name as a string. _check_no_field_is_named refuses a field called security, because it would overwrite the key column of the result.
  2. Build the request. _create_request opens //blp/refdata if this BQuery has not used it yet and returns an empty ReferenceDataRequest. _append_values fills securities and fields. _set_overrides checks the overrides (through _override_pairs) and writes them; _set_options sets each option under Bloomberg's own element name.

  3. Send it. _send_request sends the request and reads events until the RESPONSE event that ends the answer. It keeps only messages that carry the correlation ID of this request, raises BloombergError if Bloomberg refuses the request, and returns the payloads. Here that is one payload (shortened):

    {
    "securityData": [
        {
            "security": "IBM US Equity",
            "fieldData": {"NAME": "INTL BUSINESS MACHINES CORP"},
        },
        {
            "security": "NOT A SECURITY Equity",
            "securityError": {
                "category": "BAD_SEC",
                "message": "Unknown/Invalid Security  [nid:<server>]",
            },
            "fieldData": {},
        },
    ]
}

    If the BQuery was created with debug=, _write_debug_dump writes the request and the messages to a file at this point, also when the request failed.

  4. Parse the answer. _parse_bdp makes one row per security. The unknown security has no NAME in its fieldData, so its row holds None. _security_errors turns the securityError into one line of text, and _warn_security_errors logs all such lines of the call as one warning.

  5. Build the DataFrame. Two rows; NAME is null for the unknown security.

The caller sees a warning in the log and gets the DataFrame:

Bloomberg reported 1 error(s):
  NOT A SECURITY Equity: Unknown/Invalid Security  [nid:<server>] (BAD_SEC)

shape: (2, 2)
┌───────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐
│ security              ┆ NAME                        │
│ ---                   ┆ ---                         │
│ str                   ┆ str                         │
╞═══════════════════════╪═════════════════════════════╡
│ IBM US Equity         ┆ INTL BUSINESS MACHINES CORP │
│ NOT A SECURITY Equity ┆ null                        │
└───────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘

[nid:<server>] stands for the name of the Bloomberg server that answered. A recording never stores that name.

docs.title: Find where a bug is
docs.text:
A debug dump tells you which of the five steps went wrong. Run the failing call with BQuery(debug=True). Every request then writes one JSON file to debug_cases/: the request that was sent, and every message that came back. This is the dump of bq.bdp(["IBM US Equity"], ["NAME", "NOT_A_FIELD"]), shortened:

{
 "format": 1,
 "recorded": {"date": "2026-11-16", "blpapi": "3.26.10.1", "polars": "2.1.0"},
 "request": {
  "operation": "ReferenceDataRequest",
  "body": {"securities": ["IBM US Equity"], "fields": ["NAME", "NOT_A_FIELD"]}
 },
 "events": [{
   "type": "RESPONSE",
   "messages": [{
     "type": "ReferenceDataResponse",
     "payload": {"securityData": [{
       "security": "IBM US Equity",
       "fieldExceptions": [{
         "fieldId": "NOT_A_FIELD",
         "errorInfo": {"category": "BAD_FLD", "message": "Field not valid"}
       }],
       "fieldData": {"NAME": "INTL BUSINESS MACHINES CORP"}
     }]}
   }]
 }]
}

Compare the dump with what the user expected, from the top:

What you find Where to look No file was written Nothing was sent. The call failed in step 1 or in _create_request: the session is not started, or the service did not open. request is not what the user asked for Step 2: the body of the method, and section 2 of plbbg.py. request is right, but events does not hold the data, or holds an error Bloomberg did not send the data. Look for the behavior in the quirks table. If it is not there, the cause is usually the content of the request (a field, an override, an entitlement) and not the library. events holds the data, but the DataFrame lacks it, or has it under the wrong name or dtype Steps 4 and 5: the parser of the method, in sections 3 to 6. The call hangs, times out, or returns the data of another call Step 3: _send_request.

The same file is the input of an offline test. See Capture a failing case.

docs.title: Bloomberg quirks the code handles
docs.text:
Read this table before you "fix" something: what looks like a bug of the library is often a behavior of Bloomberg that the code handles on purpose. Each quirk has a comment at the place that handles it. A name like bdp/partial_responses is the recording tests/data/recordings/bdp/partial_responses.json; open it to see the raw answer. Where no recording shows the quirk, the table names a test.

Quirk Handled in Shown by Any call An answer arrives as several events _send_request bdp/partial_responses The reply to an old request that timed out arrives during the next request _send_request (correlation ID check, and the cancel on any error) test_late_answer_to_timed_out_request_is_not_returned_to_next_request in tests/unit/test_send_request.py Bloomberg refuses a request in two ways: a RequestFailure message, or a responseError inside a normal response _send_request test_request_failure_raises_bloomberg_error_with_reason in tests/unit/test_send_request.py (the first way); bdp/no_securities (the second) An override date must be sent as YYYYMMDD; Bloomberg ignores other forms without an error _override_pairs bdp/override_reference_date (the accepted form) bdp and bdh An unknown security or field does not fail the request; it is reported inside the answer _security_errors bdp/invalid_security_mixed, bdp/invalid_field_mixed, bdh/invalid_field_mixed An unknown security is a row of nulls in bdp but no rows in bdh _parse_bdp, _parse_bdh bdp/invalid_security_mixed, bdh/invalid_security_mixed bdp rows come back in Bloomberg's order, not in the order of the request _parse_bdp bdp/partial_responses Field names come back spelled as the request spelled them _parse_bdp bdp/lowercase_field bdib An unknown security fails the whole request here, with a responseError _send_request bdib/invalid_security Intraday times are UTC, in the request and in the answer _iso_datetime, _BAR_SCHEMA bdib/trade_bars_60min The intraday answer does not name the security _parse_bdib bdib/trade_bars_60min bql The request says that it comes from Excel, as Bloomberg's own Excel add-in does _set_bql_client_context test_bql_request_sets_expression_and_client_context in tests/unit/test_requests.py A BQL answer is JSON text, and a long one is cut into fragments over several messages _load_bql_answers test_bql_answer_split_over_several_messages_is_joined in tests/unit/test_bql.py A failed BQL query is an answer too, with its reason inside _parse_bql bql/syntax_error, bql/invalid_item "No results" is sent as an exception of type BENIGN _parse_bql bql/empty_universe BQL sends dates, NaN and infinity as text _bql_date, _bql_datetime, _bql_number bql/date_value, bql/nan_and_infinity A BQL item can be named like one of its own columns _bql_item bql/item_named_id bsrch A search grid has no column types; an empty numeric cell is a blank string _cell_value, _blank_strings_to_none test_bsrch_blank_cells_in_numeric_column_become_null in tests/unit/test_bsrch.py ReachMax is true also when a LIMIT override cut the search short _parse_bsrch bsrch/coco_limit_2 A failed search is a grid with an Error text _parse_bsrch bsrch/invalid_domain

docs.title: Run the checks
docs.text:
Check Command Run it Offline tests pytest before every commit Lint and format ruff check . and ruff format --check . before every commit Recordings replay to the same results python tests/record.py --refresh-expected, then git diff --stat tests/data/recordings must print nothing after a change to plbbg.py Minimum dependencies see below before a pull request that changes plbbg.py Docs build mkdocs build --strict after a change to docs/ or to a public docstring Live tests pytest --bbg when you have a Bloomberg Terminal on this machine Recipe outputs python dev/refresh_recipes.py, then review git diff docs/recipes at a Terminal, after adding or changing a recipe in docs/recipes/, or when its output is stale

A recipe in docs/recipes/ is a self-contained ```python block that prints its result, followed by a line starting with Output and a fenced block. The script runs each recipe, pastes what it printed into that block and sets the page's "as of" date. To add a recipe, write the code with an empty output block and run the script. A page with a failing recipe is not written, and that includes a screen that matches nothing on the day.

A recipe on the page looks like this; docs/stylesheets/recipes.css styles it.

## Large axes only

`axes_by_dealer()`, `matches()`, `dropna()`
{ .recipe-uses }

One sentence: the question the recipe answers.

```python
...
```

Output
``` { .text .no-copy .recipe-output }
```

!!! warning "Watch out"
    Only traps that give a wrong number or an error.

Notes
{ .recipe-label }

- How to read the output and adapt the query.
  • The { .recipe-uses } line is the "Uses" cell of the recipe's row in recipes/index.md; keep the two the same. It also numbers the heading.
  • Keep the blank line before Output. Without it the label is not a paragraph and loses its style.
  • The output block is text, not python, and has no copy button.

The recordings check repeats what pytest does, but more strictly: pytest compares numbers with a tolerance, and git diff shows every difference.

The offline tests must also pass on the oldest supported versions (Python 3.12, polars 1.7.1, blpapi 3.24.2). Build that environment outside the repository and leave the project environment alone:

MIN=~/venvs/plbbg-min    # any directory outside the repository
uv venv $MIN --python 3.12
uv pip install --python $MIN --no-config \
    --index https://blpapi.bloomberg.com/repository/releases/python/simple/ \
    --index https://pypi.org/simple \
    -e . pytest pytest-cov pyyaml "polars==1.7.1" "blpapi==3.24.2"
$MIN/bin/python -m pytest tests/unit -m no_bbg

On Windows the interpreter of that environment is Scripts\python.exe instead of bin/python.

How the tests are organised, and in which order to read the live tests as a tour of the library, is in tests/README.md.

docs.title: Capture a failing case and turn it into an offline test
docs.text:
The call and the names in this recipe are examples; use those of your case.

  1. Get the raw answer. Run the failing call with debug=True, or ask the user who reported it to do so:

    with BQuery(debug=True) as bq:
    bq.bdp(["IBM US Equity"], ["NAME", "NOT_A_FIELD"])

    Every request writes one JSON file to debug_cases/ in the working directory, for example ReferenceDataRequest_20261116_201008_297370.json, also when the call raises. The file holds the request, every message Bloomberg sent back, and the library versions; Find where a bug is shows one. BQuery(debug="some/dir") writes to that directory.

  2. Make it small and public. The repository is public. Cut the answer down by hand to what shows the problem: at most three securities and five rows where the case allows it. Replace instruments and names that are the user's own by well-known ones, in the request and in the answer alike. Keep the markers that hold dates, such as {"$date": "2024-01-02"}: the replay turns them back into dates. Never commit debug_cases/ itself.

  3. Store it as a recording. Copy the file to tests/data/recordings/<method>/<short_name>.json, and add the call under the same name to SCENARIOS in tests/recordings.py:

    "bdp/unknown_field_next_to_known": lambda bq: bq.bdp(
    ["IBM US Equity"], ["NAME", "NOT_A_FIELD"]
),

    If nobody can record this answer again (the user's own instruments, a market state that is gone), also add the name to CONVERTED in the same file. Then python tests/record.py leaves the file alone.

    From now until step 5, tests/unit/test_recordings.py fails for the new scenario with KeyError: 'expected'. That is correct: the file does not say yet what the call should give.

  4. Write the test that shows the bug, in tests/unit/test_<method>.py:

    def test_bdp_unknown_field_next_to_known_gives_a_null_column():
    bq, _ = replay("bdp/unknown_field_next_to_known")

    df = bq.bdp(["IBM US Equity"], ["NAME", "NOT_A_FIELD"])

    assert df["NOT_A_FIELD"].to_list() == [None]

    replay (in tests/support.py) returns a BQuery whose fake session answers the next request with the recorded messages. Run the test and see it fail.

  5. Fix the code, then store the result the call now gives:

    python tests/record.py --refresh-expected bdp/unknown_field_next_to_known

    This replays the answer, writes the result into the file as "expected", and replaces server names in Bloomberg's error details. Read the file once more, then run pytest: tests/unit/test_recordings.py now replays the new scenario together with all the others.

A recording made this way works like one recorded live. It differs in two harmless ways: it has no "scenario" and "call" keys, and a BQL answer stays one long JSON string instead of readable JSON.

docs.title: Fix a parsing bug
docs.text:
1. Find the parser in the method table and open a recording of that method to see the shape of the payloads.

  2. Reproduce the bug in a test. Replay a recording as in the recipe above, or write the payload by hand when a few lines are enough:

    def test_bdp_security_without_field_data_gives_a_null():
    payload = {"securityData": [{"security": "IBM US Equity", "fieldData": {}}]}
    bq = fake_bq([answer(payload)])

    df = bq.bdp(["IBM US Equity"], ["NAME"])

    assert df["NAME"].to_list() == [None]

    fake_bq and answer are in tests/support.py. The files tests/unit/test_bdp.py to test_bsrch.py show both kinds of test.

  3. Fix the parser and run pytest.

  4. Run python tests/record.py --refresh-expected and read git diff tests/data/recordings. Only the scenarios whose result you meant to change may differ.
  5. If users can notice the fix, add a line to CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: Add an option
docs.text:
A Bloomberg request option needs no new code. options={"periodicitySelection": "MONTHLY"} reaches the request through _set_options, under Bloomberg's own element name.

The offline tests build real blpapi requests on a reduced, hand-written schema, tests/data/schemas/refdata_test.xml. An option that the schema does not list raises NotFoundException there. To test a request with a new option, add the <element> to the request type in that file, then assert on the request in tests/unit/test_requests.py with request_sent_by.

A new keyword argument of a public method goes the same way as the existing ones: check it in step 1, set it in step 2, test the request in tests/unit/test_requests.py, describe it in the docstring and in docs/usage/<method>.md, and add it to CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: Add a new request type
docs.text:
1. Write the public method on BQuery in the five steps, after the method it resembles most.
  2. Add a numbered section for it below the class with its _parse_<name> function, and add the method to the table and the section list in the module docstring.
  3. Make the request testable offline. For //blp/refdata, add the operation and its request and response types to tests/data/schemas/refdata_test.xml. For another service there is no offline schema; the tests use a MagicMock service, as tests/unit/test_bsrch.py does.
  4. Add scenarios to SCENARIOS in tests/recordings.py and record them at a Terminal: python tests/record.py <name>/. List a scenario in VOLATILE if its data changes from run to run, and in CONTRACT if a live test should watch the format of its answer.
  5. Add tests/unit/test_<name>.py (offline, end to end) and tests/integration/test_integration_<name>.py (live).
  6. Document it: a Google-style docstring with an example (docs/api.md renders it), a page docs/usage/<name>.md listed in mkdocs.yml, a section in README.md, a line in CHANGELOG.md, and a row in the tables of this page.

docs.title: Re-record or refresh recordings
docs.text:
A recording is one file: the request, the raw messages, and "expected", the result the call gave.

  • You changed the output on purpose (no Terminal needed). Run python tests/record.py --refresh-expected; it replays every recording and rewrites only "expected". Add name prefixes to limit it, for example python tests/record.py --refresh-expected bql/. Review git diff tests/data/recordings before you commit.
  • You need a fresh answer from Bloomberg (Terminal needed). Run python tests/record.py bdp/ bql/syntax_error for the scenarios whose names start with these prefixes, or python tests/record.py for all. Scenarios in VOLATILE change on every run; scenarios in CONVERTED are skipped.
  • You suspect Bloomberg changed a format. pytest --bbg includes tests/integration/test_contract.py, which asks Bloomberg again for the scenarios in CONTRACT and compares the shape of the fresh answer with the recording.
  • You changed the dump format in _write_debug_dump. Every recording is a dump, so all of them have to be recorded again. Avoid it.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Users must not be surprised. Method names, parameters, column names, dtypes, exception types and the wording of log messages are part of the interface; tests assert on them. A change that users can notice goes into CHANGELOG.md.
  • One file, plain functions. Being able to open plbbg.py and follow a call from request to DataFrame is the main strength of the library. Prefer a function to a new class, and do not split the file.
  • Comments say why. When a comment explains a Bloomberg quirk, name the recording that shows it.
  • Ruff checks and formats the code (pyproject.toml): line length 89, docstrings required in the package but not in tests, at most six arguments per function.
  • Public methods keep Google-style docstrings with an example and its output.
  • Diagnostics go through logger, never print.
  • No new dependencies, at runtime or for development. Python 3.12+, polars 1.7.1+, blpapi 3.24.2+.
  • Tests check one behavior each, and the name states the scenario and the expected result, for example test_bdh_weekend_range_returns_empty_frame_with_columns. They go through the public methods with the fake session; they do not patch private functions. Offline test modules set pytestmark = pytest.mark.no_bbg, live ones pytest.mark.requires_bbg.
  • Recordings stay small and public: well-known instruments, at most three securities and five rows where the scenario allows it, no machine names.
  • Releases are the maintainer's: do not bump the version, tag or publish.

docs.title: Before you open a pull request
docs.text:
1. pytest, ruff check . and ruff format --check . pass.
  2. python tests/record.py --refresh-expected changes no recording, or only the recordings whose result you meant to change.
  3. If you changed plbbg.py, the offline tests also pass on the minimum dependencies.
  4. A bug fix comes with a test that failed before the fix.
  5. A change that users can notice has a line under "Unreleased" in CHANGELOG.md, and the docstring and the page in docs/usage/ say what the code now does.
  6. The version number is untouched.

docs.title: AT1 Bond Valuation
AT1 Bond Valuation¶
docs.text:
© 2025 Marek Ozana

This notebook is a small, opinionated workflow for relative value screening in the AT1 universe using polars-bloomberg and interactive Altair charts.

We pull a bond universe (IDs, tickers, ratings, duration, back-end spread, z-spread) and then visualize how z-spread behaves as a function of:

  • Back-end spread (BE) and
  • Duration (Dur)

Both views include a simple fit. Bonds above the trend line are “cheap” on that axis (wider than the model would suggest), and bonds below the line are “rich”.

The two scatter plots are linked: clicking a point in one chart highlights the same bond in the other view, making it easy to spot names that look cheap (or rich) in both dimensions.

docs.title: AT1 vs Credits Historical OAS per Rating
AT1 vs Credits Historical OAS per Rating¶
docs.text:
© 2025 Marek Ozana

This notebook shows how to use polars-bloomberg to pull BQL history and compare option-adjusted spreads (OAS) between AT1 (CoCo) bonds and other (non-subordinated) credit, bucketed by rating. The BQL query is constructed to pull historical OAS by date, rating, and credit type (CoCo vs Credit). By controlling for credit risk via rating, we can isolate the “AT1 premium” and show that CoCo investors have historically earned additional spread even after adjusting for credit quality.

We:

  • Pull historical OAS for AT1 (CoCo) and senior credit across rating buckets

  • Chart the spread gap through time to highlight the persistent CoCo premium after rating adjustment

docs.title: CET1 vs Requirements and AT1 Trigger levels
CET1 vs Requirements and AT1 Trigger levels¶
docs.text:
© 2025 Marek Ozana

This notebook is a small end-to-end example of using polars-bloomberg to pull regulatory capital metrics from BQL and chart them for a universe of European banks.

We compare three CET1-related levels:

  • CET1 (reported): the bank’s current Common Equity Tier 1 ratio (what it has).
  • CET1 requirement (“review” / SREP): the supervisory CET1 requirement level (what it must meet under review-driven requirements).
  • AT1 trigger: the contractual CET1 trigger level associated with Additional Tier 1 (CoCo) instruments (the “oh no” line where conversion/write-down mechanics may be activated).

Interpretation:

  • The vertical gap CET1 − requirement is “headroom” against supervisory requirements.
  • The gap CET1 − AT1 trigger is distance to the contractual AT1 trigger (not a regulatory buffer).
  • Field definitions vary by jurisdiction and data source. Treat these as indicative and sanity-check against bank disclosures when precision matters.

docs.title: Bank Capital, Asset Quality and Profitability¶
docs.text:
© 2025 Marek Ozana

This notebook pulls quarterly fundamentals for a panel of large European banks and visualizes three core health signals:

  • Capital (CET1 ratio): how much loss-absorbing capital banks have (higher is better)
  • Asset quality (NPL ratio): how much of the loan book is non-performing (lower is better)
  • Profitability (ROE): how efficiently equity is turned into earnings (higher is better)

In the chart below, the line shows the cross-bank average over time and the shaded band shows the dispersion across banks. The big picture is simple: European banks are currently better capitalized, have cleaner loan books (lower NPLs), and are generating higher ROE than in most of the post-crisis period.

docs.title: Credit Spreads vs Equity Cushion
Credit Spreads vs Equity Cushion¶
docs.text:
© 2025 Marek Ozana

This notebook uses polars-bloomberg to study how bond spreads relate to a company’s equity cushion, (EV-NetDebt) / EV

We plot each issuer as a scatter point using average z-spread per year of duration versus equity cushion and highlight the typical “hockey-stick” pattern: spreads are fairly stable at healthy cushions, then widen rapidly when the cushion becomes thin.

Implementation detail: in Bloomberg BQL we map each bond to its issuer fundamentals via fundamentalTicker (mapby=LINEAGE), then group by ticker and rating to aggregate bond-level spread/duration and issuer-level fundamentals into one issuer datapoint.

docs.title: Central Bank Policy Rates - History vs. Forecast¶
docs.text:
© 2026 Jim Domeij

The chart shows quarterly policy rates from 2019 onward for the US (Fed), Eurozone (ECB), UK (BoE), and Japan (BoJ), extended with Bloomberg’s median economist forecasts through 2027. Solid line segments represent realized (actual) policy settings, while dashed segments show the current consensus expected path as of the data pull date. Comparing levels and slopes highlights where markets expect tightening, easing, or prolonged stability—and how the projected policy divergence/convergence evolves across regions.

docs.title: Historical FED Policy Rates vs Expectations¶
docs.text:
© 2026 Jim Domeij & Marek Ozana

This chart reconstructs how expectations for the Fed funds rate evolved over time. Each line is a year-end snapshot (AS_OF_DATE) of Bloomberg’s median economist path for future policy rates, shown alongside realized settings. Solid segments indicate historical (actual) policy rates, while dashed segments show the forecast that was in place on that snapshot date.

docs.title: Central-bank rate changes (G20)
Central-bank rate changes (G20)¶
docs.text:
© 2026 Jim Domeij

Each month, we count how many G20 central banks raised their policy rate (hikes) and how many lowered it (cuts), as a simple proxy for the breadth of global tightening vs easing.

The top panel shows hikes (up) and cuts (down). The bottom panel shows the net balance on the same scale.

Note: This is a count of central banks changing rates, not the magnitude of the rate moves.

docs.title: Regional PE Valuation
Regional PE Valuation¶
docs.text:
© 2026 Jim Domeij

This calculates 10-year P/E valuation statistics (average, standard deviation, minimum and maximum) for major equity regions. Current levels are compared to these statistics to assess the relative expansiveness vs history and other regions.

The BQL query builds a shared 10-year date range, defines a reusable forward P/E series, and computes #avg, #std, #min, #max, plus the latest value #last for each index in the universe. BQL returns a Polars DataFrame with ID and those five fields, which are renamed for plotting.

The chart visualizes each region’s distribution using a box for average ±1 standard deviation, whiskers for min/max, a diamond for the average, and a triangle for the latest value.

docs.title: S&P 500 Earning Revisions Breadth
S&P 500 Earning Revisions Breadth¶
docs.text:
© 2025 Jim Domeij & Marek Ozana

This calculates, for each GICS sector within the S&P 500, the number of companies with upward or downward EPS revisions over the past month. It can be used to track the breadth of change in analysts’ EPS estimates by sector.

docs.title: S&P 500 Valuation Scenarios
S&P 500 Valuation Scenarios¶
docs.text:
© 2025 Jim Domeij & Marek Ozana

This chart shows potential S&P 500 price levels and returns for the next 12 months. It uses a scenario matrix driven by two factors: Forward P/E ratios (vertical axis, from historical averages) and Forward EPS growth (horizontal axis, centered on consensus). Each cell displays the resulting index price and percentage return from the current price. This helps investors visualize risk and potential upside under different market conditions.

docs.title: US Economic Data Surprises¶
docs.text:
© 2026 Jim Domeij

Uses the powerful calendar() function to retrieve US economic data releases from the past two month across multiple sectors, excluding low-relevance series and assessing how each release has surprised relative to Bloomberg’s median survey forecast. This provides an overview of recent US economic momentum versus consensus expectations, with the ability to drill down into the details of individual data releases.

In BQL, calendar() enables bulk retrieval of historical and upcoming economic releases from a comprehensive global dataset covering more than 2,000 events across 100+ countries, with data extending back to 1997.

SURPRISE is defined as (actual value - survey median) / survey standard deviation.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text:
Short reference queries grouped by workflow. Each recipe has the query, the Python code that runs it and the output it printed.

For how bql() and combine() work, see BQL; for bdh(), see BDH. For worked analyses with charts, see the Examples.

docs.title: Workflows
docs.text:
• New Issues

    New AT1, RT1 and Technology deals in the primary pipeline, and the pipeline by currency.

    BQL 3 recipes

  • Dealer Axes

    What dealers want to buy or sell: per bond, per dealer and per issuer, today and over 1 and 5 weeks, next to spreads.

    BQL 7 recipes

  • Bonds and Capital Structure

    Bank capital stacks, call schedules, distance to the AT1 trigger, debt by rank with leverage, and the CAST parent.

    BQL 7 recipes

  • Spread Statistics

    OAS per rating and the AT1 premium, monthly and daily spread history, index yield vs OAS, and YAS at any price.

    BQL YAS 7 recipes

  • Company Fundamentals

    From a bond to the company that reports: revenue, EBITDA, segments, bank CET1 and ROE, leverage per sector.

    BQL BSRCH 8 recipes

  • Market History with BDH

    Weekly spreads, holiday calendars, fund flows, CDS basis, hedged yields, fiscal-year leverage and candles.

    BDH 7 recipes

docs.title: How to read a recipe
docs.text:
1. Question: the heading and the line under it say what the recipe answers.
  2. Uses: the functions and options it shows.
  3. Code: copy it with the button and run it at a Bloomberg Terminal.
  4. Output: what it printed on the date at the top of the page.
  5. Watch out: traps that give wrong numbers, often without an error.
  6. Notes: how to read the output and adapt the query.

docs.title: Dealer Axes
docs.text:
An axe is a dealer's signal that it wants to buy (bid) or sell (ask) a bond. BQL returns the axes you see in IMGR AXE <GO> and QMGR AXE <GO>, so you can rank, join and chart them in Python.

Data on this page

Every recipe uses the same universe: the USD AT1 bonds of Swedish banks, a handful of SEB, Handelsbanken and Swedbank perpetuals. For other bonds, change the for() clause. Sizes are face amounts in the bond's currency.

The outputs below are live data as of 2026-11-17 and will differ when you run the queries.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: You want Use One row per Is the bond axed, by how many dealers, total size per side axes() bond Each dealer's axe: dealer, size, price, spread, yield axes_by_dealer() dealer and bond Axe size over the last week or five weeks axes(calc_interval=1w) or 5w, columns BID_HIST_AGG_SIZE, ASK_HIST_AGG_SIZE bond Only bonds that have live axes universe axedUniv('all') (or 'bid', 'ask'), filter is_axed() bond

docs.title: AT1 axes by bond
docs.text:
axes()

Which bonds are axed, by how many dealers, and for how much in total.

from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
get(name, axes() as #ax)
for(filter(bondsUniv(ACTIVE),
        crncy() == 'USD' and country_iso() == 'SE' and
        basel_iii_designation() == 'Additional Tier 1'))
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine(on="ID")
print(df)

Output

┌───────────────┬─────────────────┬─────┬───────────┬───────────┬────────────────┬────────────────┐
│ ID            ┆ name            ┆ #ax ┆ ASK_DEPTH ┆ BID_DEPTH ┆ ASK_TOTAL_SIZE ┆ BID_TOTAL_SIZE │

│ str           ┆ str             ┆ str ┆ i64       ┆ i64       ┆ f64            ┆ f64            │

│ BR069680 Corp ┆ SWEDA 4 PERP    ┆ Y   ┆ null      ┆ 9         ┆ null           ┆ 2e7            │
│ BW924993 Corp ┆ SEB 6 ⅞ PERP    ┆ Y   ┆ 1         ┆ 6         ┆ 2e6            ┆ 3.3e7          │
│ DL161992 Corp ┆ SEB 6 ¾ PERP    ┆ Y   ┆ 5         ┆ null      ┆ 1.22e7         ┆ null           │
│ YU819930 Corp ┆ SEB 6 ¾ PERP    ┆ Y   ┆ 1         ┆ 1         ┆ 5e6            ┆ 1e6            │
│ ZF859199 Corp ┆ SWEDA 7 ¾ PERP  ┆ Y   ┆ 1         ┆ 7         ┆ 1e6            ┆ 3.1e7          │
│ ZL122341 Corp ┆ SWEDA 7 ⅝ PERP  ┆ Y   ┆ 2         ┆ 1         ┆ 8e6            ┆ 3e6            │

Notes

  • #ax is Y when the bond has at least one live axe.
  • BID_DEPTH is the number of dealers bidding and BID_TOTAL_SIZE the sum of their sizes; ASK_* is the same for the offer side. A null side has no axes.
  • preferences(addcols=all) adds more columns, among them one dealer's price, spread and yield, and the 1-week *_HIST_AGG_SIZE.
  • To start from axed bonds only, use axedUniv('all') instead of bondsUniv(ACTIVE).

docs.title: Large axes only
docs.text:
axes_by_dealer(), matches(), dropna()

Dealer axes of 10 million or more, filtered by Bloomberg before the data is sent.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
let(#axe = axes_by_dealer();
    #large = dropna(matches(#axe, #axe().bid_size >= 10M or #axe().ask_size >= 10M),
                    remove_id=True);)
get(name, #large)
for(filter(bondsUniv(ACTIVE),
        crncy() == 'USD' and country_iso() == 'SE' and
        basel_iii_designation() == 'Additional Tier 1'))
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine(on="ID", how="inner")
print(
    df.select(
        "name",
        dealer=pl.coalesce("BID_DEALER", "ASK_DEALER"),
        bid_mm=pl.col("BID_SIZE") / 1e6,
        ask_mm=pl.col("ASK_SIZE") / 1e6,
        bid_px="BID_PRICE",
        ask_px="ASK_PRICE",
    ).sort("name", "dealer")
)

Output 

shape: (4, 6)
┌─────────────────┬────────┬────────┬────────┬─────────┬────────┐
│ name            ┆ dealer ┆ bid_mm ┆ ask_mm ┆ bid_px  ┆ ask_px │
│ ---             ┆ ---    ┆ ---    ┆ ---    ┆ ---     ┆ ---    │
│ str             ┆ str    ┆ f64    ┆ f64    ┆ f64     ┆ f64    │
╞═════════════════╪════════╪════════╪════════╪═════════╪════════╡
│ SEB 6 ⅞ PERP    ┆ HSBC   ┆ 15.0   ┆ null   ┆ 100.25  ┆ null   │
│ SHBASS 4 ⅜ PERP ┆ HSBC   ┆ 15.0   ┆ null   ┆ 99.5    ┆ null   │
│ SHBASS 4 ⅜ PERP ┆ ING    ┆ 10.0   ┆ null   ┆ 99.35   ┆ null   │
│ SWEDA 7 ¾ PERP  ┆ MS     ┆ 10.0   ┆ null   ┆ 101.875 ┆ null   │
└─────────────────┴────────┴────────┴────────┴─────────┴────────┘

Watch out

Compare dealers on price or yield. A dealer's spread can be 0 or quoted on another basis.

Notes

  • axes_by_dealer() has one row per dealer and bond. Most dealers are axed on one side only, so the other side is null.
  • matches() keeps the rows that pass the test and dropna(..., remove_id=True) removes the others. how="inner" then keeps only the bonds with a large axe.
  • 10M is BQL shorthand for 10,000,000, and K stands for thousands.

docs.title: Net axes per issuer
docs.text:
sum(group(..., ticker))

Are dealers buyers or sellers of each issuer's AT1s? A bid axe is a dealer that wants to buy, an ask axe a dealer that wants to sell.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
get(sum(group(axes().bid_total_size, ticker)) / 1M as #bid,
    sum(group(axes().ask_total_size, ticker)) / 1M as #ask)
for(filter(bondsUniv(ACTIVE),
        crncy() == 'USD' and country_iso() == 'SE' and
        basel_iii_designation() == 'Additional Tier 1'))
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine(on="ID")
net = pl.col("#bid").fill_null(0) - pl.col("#ask").fill_null(0)
print(
    df.select(
        issuer="ID",
        bid_mm="#bid",
        ask_mm="#ask",
        net_mm=net,
        dealers=pl.when(net > 0).then(pl.lit("buyers")).otherwise(pl.lit("sellers")),
    )
)

Output 

shape: (3, 5)
┌────────┬────────┬────────┬────────┬─────────┐
│ issuer ┆ bid_mm ┆ ask_mm ┆ net_mm ┆ dealers │
│ ---    ┆ ---    ┆ ---    ┆ ---    ┆ ---     │
│ str    ┆ f64    ┆ f64    ┆ f64    ┆ str     │
╞════════╪════════╪════════╪════════╪═════════╡
│ SEB    ┆ 34.0   ┆ 19.2   ┆ 14.8   ┆ buyers  │
│ SHBASS ┆ 49.2   ┆ 14.6   ┆ 34.6   ┆ buyers  │
│ SWEDA  ┆ 54.0   ┆ 9.0    ┆ 45.0   ┆ buyers  │
└────────┴────────┴────────┴────────┴─────────┘

Watch out

/ 1M turns the sizes into millions. Sizes add up in each bond's own currency; for bonds in several currencies, add with(currency=USD).

Notes

  • With group(..., ticker) the ID column holds the ticker, not a bond.

docs.title: Total axes: today, 1 week, 5 weeks
docs.text:
calc_interval, *_HIST_AGG_SIZE

All bid and ask axes on the universe, now and over the last one and five weeks.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
get(sum(group(axes().bid_total_size)) / 1M as #bid_today,
    sum(group(axes().ask_total_size)) / 1M as #ask_today,
    sum(group(axes(calc_interval=1w).bid_hist_agg_size)) / 1M as #bid_1w,
    sum(group(axes(calc_interval=1w).ask_hist_agg_size)) / 1M as #ask_1w,
    sum(group(axes(calc_interval=5w).bid_hist_agg_size)) / 1M as #bid_5w,
    sum(group(axes(calc_interval=5w).ask_hist_agg_size)) / 1M as #ask_5w)
for(filter(bondsUniv(ACTIVE),
        crncy() == 'USD' and country_iso() == 'SE' and
        basel_iii_designation() == 'Additional Tier 1'))
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    row = bq.bql(query).combine(on="ID").row(0, named=True)
windows = ["today", "1w", "5w"]
df = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "window": windows,
        "bid_mm": [row[f"#bid_{w}"] for w in windows],
        "ask_mm": [row[f"#ask_{w}"] for w in windows],
    }
).with_columns(net_mm=pl.col("bid_mm") - pl.col("ask_mm"))
print(df)

Output 

shape: (3, 4)
┌────────┬─────────┬────────┬────────┐
│ window ┆ bid_mm  ┆ ask_mm ┆ net_mm │
│ ---    ┆ ---     ┆ ---    ┆ ---    │
│ str    ┆ f64     ┆ f64    ┆ f64    │
╞════════╪═════════╪════════╪════════╡
│ today  ┆ 137.2   ┆ 42.8   ┆ 94.4   │
│ 1w     ┆ 177.44  ┆ 58.76  ┆ 118.68 │
│ 5w     ┆ 143.756 ┆ 73.648 ┆ 70.108 │
└────────┴─────────┴────────┴────────┘

Watch out

BQL has no day-by-day axe history: calc_interval takes only 1w and 5w, axes(dates=...) is rejected and with(dates=...) has no effect. For a daily series, store the output of the first recipe every day.

Notes

  • group() without a key puts every bond in one group, whose ID is IdentityGroup.
  • *_HIST_AGG_SIZE is on the same scale as today's *_TOTAL_SIZE (the 5-week value is not five times the 1-week value), so the rows compare directly.

docs.title: Axes in a relative-value screen
docs.text:
flt_spread(), spread(spread_type=OAS)

Spreads next to axes: can you buy the cheap bonds, and sell the rich ones?

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
get(name, nxt_call_dt,
    flt_spread().value as #back_end,
    spread(spread_type=OAS).value as #oas,
    axes() as #ax)
for(filter(bondsUniv(ACTIVE),
        crncy() == 'USD' and country_iso() == 'SE' and
        basel_iii_designation() == 'Additional Tier 1'))
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine(on="ID")
print(
    df.select(
        "name",
        call="nxt_call_dt",
        back_end="#back_end",
        oas=pl.col("#oas").round(0),
        bid_mm=pl.col("BID_TOTAL_SIZE") / 1e6,
        ask_mm=pl.col("ASK_TOTAL_SIZE") / 1e6,
    ).sort("oas", descending=True)
)

Output

docs.title: Top 3 dealers
docs.text:
axes_by_dealer()

The dealers with the most axes on these bonds, bid and ask together.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
get(axes_by_dealer())
for(filter(bondsUniv(ACTIVE),
        crncy() == 'USD' and country_iso() == 'SE' and
        basel_iii_designation() == 'Additional Tier 1'))
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query)[0]
top = (
    df.group_by(dealer=pl.coalesce("BID_DEALER", "ASK_DEALER"))
    .agg(
        bonds=pl.col("ID").n_unique(),
        bid_mm=pl.col("BID_SIZE").sum() / 1e6,
        ask_mm=pl.col("ASK_SIZE").sum() / 1e6,
    )
    .with_columns(total_mm=pl.col("bid_mm") + pl.col("ask_mm"))
    .sort(["total_mm", "dealer"], descending=[True, False])
    .head(3)
)
print(top)

docs.title: Bonds and Capital Structure
docs.text:
Which bonds and loans does a company have, how do they rank, who owns the issuer, and how much debt sits at each level?

Data on this page

This page answers these questions for the three large Swedish banks, for a European high-yield issuer (Virgin Media O2) and for a group with several issuers (Heimstaden).

Amounts are converted to EUR so that they add up across currencies. The outputs below are live data as of 2026-11-17 and will differ when you run the queries. Before you adapt a query, read the Pitfalls.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text:
By taskParent types You want Use One row per All live bonds of an issuer filter(bondsUniv(ACTIVE, consolidateduplicates=True), ticker in [...]) bond Its loans filter(loansUniv(ACTIVE), ticker == '...') loan Where a bond ranks normalized_payment_rank() (comparable across issuers), payment_rank() (as issued), basel_iii_designation() (bank capital) bond Debt per rank, per issuer or per parent sum(group(amt_outstanding(currency=EUR), ...)) group The company that owns the issuer parent(type=DIRECT), type=ULTIMATE or type=CAST company The parent's fundamentals next to each bond value(<field>, parent(type=CAST), mapby=LINEAGE) bond

The capital structure (CAST) parent is the top company of the capital structure you see in CAST <GO>. Unlike the ultimate parent, it stops below private-equity sponsors, owners that hold the company as an investment, and governments that guarantee less than half of the group's debt. Since May 2026 BQL's parent() returns it with type=CAST.

parent(type=...) Returns DIRECT (default) the immediate parent company ULTIMATE the company that ultimately controls the issuer CAST the top of the capital structure in CAST <GO>

docs.title: Swedish bank capital stacks
docs.text:
normalized_payment_rank(), sum(group(..., [ticker, #rank]))

Covered bonds, senior, senior non-preferred, Tier 2 and AT1 outstanding for SEB, Handelsbanken and Swedbank, in EUR billions.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
let(#rank = normalized_payment_rank().value;
    #amt = group(amt_outstanding(currency=EUR).value / 1B, [ticker, #rank]);)
get(sum(#amt) as #eur_bn)
for(filter(bondsUniv(ACTIVE, consolidateduplicates=True),
           ticker in ['SEB', 'SHBASS', 'SWEDA']))
"""
layers = {
    "Secured": "1 Secured (covered)",
    "Sr Unsecured": "2 Senior preferred",
    "Senior Bail-In": "3 Senior non-preferred",
    "Subordinated Unsecured": "4 Tier 2",
    "Jr Subordinated Unsecured": "5 AT1",
}
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine()
print(
    df.with_columns(
        layer=pl.col("#RANK").replace(layers), eur_bn=pl.col("#eur_bn").round(1)
    )
    .pivot(on="TICKER", index="layer", values="eur_bn")
    .sort("layer")
)

Output 

shape: (5, 4)
┌────────────────────────┬──────┬────────┬───────┐
│ layer                  ┆ SEB  ┆ SHBASS ┆ SWEDA │
│ ---                    ┆ ---  ┆ ---    ┆ ---   │
│ str                    ┆ f64  ┆ f64    ┆ f64   │
╞════════════════════════╪══════╪════════╪═══════╡
│ 1 Secured (covered)    ┆ 32.0 ┆ 56.8   ┆ 36.8  │
│ 2 Senior preferred     ┆ 11.7 ┆ 27.0   ┆ 14.3  │
│ 3 Senior non-preferred ┆ 12.0 ┆ 7.6    ┆ 12.5  │
│ 4 Tier 2               ┆ 2.8  ┆ 2.3    ┆ 2.8   │
│ 5 AT1                  ┆ 1.9  ┆ 1.4    ┆ 1.5   │
└────────────────────────┴──────┴────────┴───────┘

Watch out

Swedish banks also issue structured notes and MTNs under the same ticker, so the senior preferred counts are large.

Notes

  • normalized_payment_rank() maps each bond to one ladder, the same for all issuers. Senior Bail-In is senior non-preferred (MREL), Subordinated is Tier 2 and Jr Subordinated is AT1.
  • The group column comes back as #RANK (upper case) and the ticker as TICKER.
  • consolidateduplicates=True keeps one line per bond instead of one per listing.

docs.title: AT1 and Tier 2 call schedule
docs.text:
basel_iii_designation(), nxt_call_dt

How much AT1 and Tier 2 each bank can call per year, in EUR millions.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
get(ticker, basel_iii_designation, nxt_call_dt,
    amt_outstanding(currency=EUR).value / 1M as #eur_m)
for(filter(bondsUniv(ACTIVE, consolidateduplicates=True),
           ticker in ['SEB', 'SHBASS', 'SWEDA'] and
           basel_iii_designation() in ['Additional Tier 1', 'Tier 2']))
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine()
tier = pl.col("basel_iii_designation").replace(
    {"Additional Tier 1": "AT1", "Tier 2": "T2"}
)
print(
    df.with_columns(
        bank_tier=pl.col("ticker") + " " + tier,
        call_year=pl.col("nxt_call_dt").dt.year(),
        eur_m=pl.col("#eur_m").round().cast(pl.Int64),
    )
    .sort("bank_tier")
    .pivot(on="bank_tier", index="call_year", values="eur_m", aggregate_function="sum")
    .sort("call_year")
)

The USD AT1s of the Swedish banks (the bonds on the Dealer Axes page), each with its bank's CET1 ratio and the bond's trigger, in percent of risk-weighted assets.

           basel_iii_designation() == 'Additional Tier 1'))

docs.title: Bonds and loans with leverage
docs.text:
loansUniv(ACTIVE), ebitda(fpt=LTM)

The whole debt stack of Virgin Media O2, bonds and term loans, by rank. Leverage is the debt up to and including each rank divided by last-twelve-months EBITDA.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

fields = """
get(name, maturity, normalized_payment_rank().value as #rank,
    amt_outstanding(currency=EUR).value / 1M as #eur_m)
"""
bonds = "for(filter(bondsUniv(ACTIVE, consolidateduplicates=True), ticker == 'VMED'))"
loans = "for(filter(loansUniv(ACTIVE), ticker == 'VMED' and amt_outstanding() > 0))"
parent = """
get(name, ebitda(fpt=LTM, currency=EUR) / 1M as #ebitda)
for(parent('ZO388622 Corp', type=CAST))
"""
seniority = {"1st Lien Secured": 1, "Secured": 2, "Sr Unsecured": 3}
with BQuery() as bq:
    debt = pl.concat(
        [
            bq.bql(fields + bonds).combine().with_columns(kind=pl.lit("bond")),
            bq.bql(fields + loans).combine().with_columns(kind=pl.lit("loan")),
        ]
    )
    group = bq.bql(parent).combine()
ebitda = group["#ebitda"].item()
print(
    f"{group['name'].item()}: LTM EBITDA EUR {ebitda:,.0f}m ({group['PERIOD_END_DATE'].item()})"
)
print(
    debt.group_by("#rank")
    .agg(
        bonds=(pl.col("kind") == "bond").sum(),
        loans=(pl.col("kind") == "loan").sum(),
        eur_m=pl.col("#eur_m").sum().round().cast(pl.Int64),
    )
    .sort(pl.col("#rank").replace_strict(seniority, default=9))
    .with_columns(cum_leverage=(pl.col("eur_m").cum_sum() / ebitda).round(1))
)

Output 

Vmed O2 UK Ltd: LTM EBITDA EUR 3,186m (2025-12-31)
shape: (3, 5)
┌──────────────────┬───────┬───────┬───────┬──────────────┐
│ #rank            ┆ bonds ┆ loans ┆ eur_m ┆ cum_leverage │
│ ---              ┆ ---   ┆ ---   ┆ ---   ┆ ---          │
│ str              ┆ u32   ┆ u32   ┆ i64   ┆ f64          │
╞══════════════════╪═══════╪═══════╪═══════╪══════════════╡
│ 1st Lien Secured ┆ 5     ┆ 15    ┆ 18972 ┆ 6.0          │
│ Secured          ┆ 12    ┆ 0     ┆ 10120 ┆ 9.1          │
│ Sr Unsecured     ┆ 2     ┆ 0     ┆ 1314  ┆ 9.5          │
└──────────────────┴───────┴───────┴───────┴──────────────┘

Watch out

  • Put the currency on the item, ebitda(..., currency=EUR), or use with(currency=EUR). with(ccy=EUR) is ignored without an error, and the numbers stay in the reporting currency. Check the CURRENCY column.
  • The order comes from Bloomberg's normalized rank. Read it as a debt stack, not a legal waterfall: debt of neighbouring ranks can share the same collateral.

Notes

  • parent('ZO388622 Corp', type=CAST) turns one bond into its group, Vmed O2 UK Ltd, whose accounts cover all the issuing entities.
  • Private groups report less often; PERIOD_END_DATE shows which accounts you got.
  • loans() on the parent returns nothing for this group, so the loans come from loansUniv(ACTIVE) by ticker. amt_outstanding() > 0 drops repaid and undrawn facilities.
  • Some VMED bonds are vendor-financing notes issued by separate vehicles. Use issuer() to see the issuing entity of each bond.

docs.title: Direct, ultimate and CAST parent
docs.text:
parent(type=DIRECT), ULTIMATE, CAST

Heimstaden has two bond issuers: Heimstaden AB and its residential subsidiary Heimstaden Bostad. The three parent types answer "who owns this?" differently.

from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
get(name, issuer(),
    value(name, parent(type=DIRECT), mapby=LINEAGE) as #direct,
    value(name, parent(type=ULTIMATE), mapby=LINEAGE) as #ultimate,
    value(name, parent(type=CAST), mapby=LINEAGE) as #cast)
for(['BJ158441 Corp', 'BR871064 Corp'])
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine(on="ID")
print(df.select("ID", "name", "issuer()", "#direct", "#ultimate", "#cast"))

Output 

shape: (2, 6)
┌───────────────┬─────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬───────────────┐
│ ID            ┆ name                ┆ issuer()             ┆ #direct              ┆ #ultimate            ┆ #cast         │
│ ---           ┆ ---                 ┆ ---                  ┆ ---                  ┆ ---                  ┆ ---           │
│ str           ┆ str                 ┆ str                  ┆ str                  ┆ str                  ┆ str           │
╞═══════════════╪═════════════════════╪══════════════════════╪══════════════════════╪══════════════════════╪═══════════════╡
│ BJ158441 Corp ┆ HEIBOS 2.8 05/04/35 ┆ HEIMSTADEN BOSTAD AB ┆ Heimstaden Bostad AB ┆ Heimstaden Bostad AB ┆ Heimstaden AB │
│ BR871064 Corp ┆ HEIMST 6 ¾ PERP     ┆ HEIMSTADEN AB        ┆ Fredensborg AS       ┆ Fredensborg 1994 AS  ┆ Heimstaden AB │

  • For the Heimstaden AB bond the ultimate parent is its owner, Fredensborg. The CAST parent stays at Heimstaden AB, the top of the capital structure.
  • For the Heimstaden Bostad bond the CAST parent is Heimstaden AB, which consolidates Bostad. Both issuers belong to one capital structure.
  • for(parent('BJ158441 Corp', type=CAST)) makes the parent the universe, so you can ask for its fundamentals directly.

Watch out

  • bonds('<company>') returns the bonds of that company only, not of its subsidiaries, so start from the tickers and let #cast show what belongs together.
  • dropCols=['ORIG_IDS'] matters: a group with one bond carries ORIG_IDS in count() but not in sum(), and the two items would not join.

Notes

  • Jr Subordinated here are hybrid bonds, which rank below all senior debt of the same issuer. Heimstaden AB's debt is also structurally below Bostad's, because Heimstaden AB is a holding company.

docs.title: Largest capital structures in a high-yield index
docs.text:
sum(group(..., #cast)) over members()

The ten CAST parents with the most debt in the Bloomberg Pan-European High Yield index, with their share of the index.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
let(#cast = value(name, parent(type=CAST), mapby=LINEAGE);
    #amt = group(amt_outstanding(currency=EUR).value / 1B, #cast);)
get(sum(#amt) as #eur_bn, count(#amt) as #bonds)
for(members('LP01TREU Index'))
preferences(dropCols=['ORIG_IDS'])
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine(on="ID")
print(
    df.select(
        "#CAST",
        "#bonds",
        eur_bn=pl.col("#eur_bn").round(1),
        share_pct=(100 * pl.col("#eur_bn") / pl.col("#eur_bn").sum()).round(1),
    )
    .filter(pl.col("#CAST").is_not_null())
    .sort("eur_bn", descending=True)
    .head(10)
)

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
What surprised us while writing these recipes.

Symptom Cause Fix A bond appears on two rows after combine() mapby=LINEAGE adds SOURCE_ID, which differs between items combine(on="ID"), or preferences(dropCols=['SOURCE_ID']) Thousands of rows from a parent universe A security without a parent returns the ID NULL_ID, a string that matches itself in every join Drop NULL_ID rows before combining, or keep one item Fundamentals in GBP or SEK although you asked for EUR with(ccy=EUR) leaves them in the reporting currency, without an error with(currency=EUR) or field(currency=EUR); check CURRENCY bonds('<parent>') misses the subsidiaries' bonds bonds() does not follow the CAST group: Heimstaden AB's list has no Heimstaden Bostad bonds Start from tickers or an index and group by parent(type=CAST) Screening all bonds of a country by CAST parent times out The parent is looked up for every bond in the universe Narrow the universe first (tickers, an index), then group Grouped items do not line up One-bond groups carry ORIG_IDS in some items only preferences(dropCols=['ORIG_IDS'])

docs.title: Company Fundamentals
docs.text:
A bond has no EBITDA. Often its issuer has none either. Virgin Media O2 issues bonds through eight vehicles, and the accounts a credit analyst reads belong to none of them. So before you ask for leverage, you have to find the company that reports it. BQL's fundamentalTicker() does that for bonds and loans.

Changed in May 2026

In May 2026 Bloomberg changed how it chooses that company. It now skips financing vehicles and SPVs, and it prefers operating or holding companies with current, frequently reported accounts.

Data on this page

This page starts from bonds, as a credit investor does. It covers European high-yield issuers (Virgin Media O2, INEOS, Altice, Telecom Italia, iliad), the AT1 issuers SEB, Handelsbanken and Swedbank, and the Bloomberg Pan-European High Yield index.

Amounts are in millions. The outputs below are live data as of 2026-11-17 and will differ when you run the queries. Before you adapt a query, read the Pitfalls.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text:
By taskPeriod parameters You want Use One row per The company whose accounts cover a bond or loan fundamentalTicker(<bonds>) as the universe company A company's figure next to each bond value(<field>, fundamentalticker, mapby=LINEAGE) bond Annual, half-year, quarterly or LTM figures with(fa_period_type=A, fa_period_offset=range(-1Y, 0Y)), fpt=S, Q, LTM company and period Reported or adjusted figures fa_adjusted=N or Y; fa_act_est_data=A for actuals company and period Revenue per business line or country segments('<equity>', type=reported, hierarchy=PRODUCT) or hierarchy=LOCATION segment and period Bank capital and profitability bs_tier1_com_equity_ratio(), normalized_roe() with fpt=Q bank and quarter A statistic per sector median(group(<field>, classification_name(BCLASS, 3))) over the index's companies sector Bloomberg Intelligence's sector figures bq.bsrch("BI:TPD", overrides={"BIKEY": ...}) row of the template

The period parameters work on any fundamental field, either in with(...) for the whole query or on one field, as in ebitda(fpt=LTM).

Parameter Short Example values Meaning fa_period_type fpt A, S, Q, LTM annual, half-year, quarter, last twelve months fa_period_offset fpo 0, -1, range(-3Q, 0Q) periods counted back from the company's latest report fa_period_reference fpr 2026Q3, range(2026Q1, 2026Q3) calendar periods, the same for every company fa_adjusted N, Y as reported, or Bloomberg-adjusted fa_act_est_data A, E actuals or estimates currency EUR the currency of the result; check the CURRENCY column

docs.title: From a bond to the company that reports
docs.text:
value(..., fundamentalticker, mapby=LINEAGE)

For each ticker, the issuing entities of its live bonds, the company whose accounts fundamentalTicker uses, and the capital structure (CAST) parent.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
let(#accounts = value(name, fundamentalticker, mapby=LINEAGE);
    #cast = value(name, parent(type=CAST), mapby=LINEAGE);)
get(ticker, issuer(), #accounts, #cast)
for(filter(bondsUniv(ACTIVE, consolidateduplicates=True),
           ticker in ['VMED', 'INEGRP', 'ALTICE', 'TITIM', 'ILDFP', 'HEIBOS', 'SEB']))
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine(on="ID")
print(
    df.group_by("ticker", "#accounts", "#cast")
    .agg(issuers=pl.col("issuer()").n_unique(), bonds=pl.len())
    .sort("ticker", "bonds", descending=[False, True])
)

The accounts stay with Telecom Italia, which reports them. The CAST parent is the top of the capital structure; fundamentalTicker is the company whose figures matter for the bond.

docs.title: Annual revenue and EBITDA, last two years
docs.text:
fundamentalticker(...), fa_period_type=A, fa_period_offset=range(-1Y, 0Y)

Revenue, EBITDA and EBITDA margin of the high-yield companies above, for the last two fiscal years, in EUR millions.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
get(name, sales_rev_turn / 1M as #revenue, ebitda / 1M as #ebitda)
for(fundamentalticker(filter(bondsUniv(ACTIVE, consolidateduplicates=True),
                             ticker in ['VMED', 'INEGRP', 'ALTICE', 'TITIM', 'ILDFP'])))
with(fa_period_type=A, fa_period_offset=range(-1Y, 0Y), currency=EUR)
preferences(dropCols=['AS_OF_DATE', 'REVISION_DATE'])
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine()
table = df.sort("name", "PERIOD_END_DATE").select(
    "name",
    "PERIOD_END_DATE",
    revenue=pl.col("#revenue").round().cast(pl.Int64),
    ebitda=pl.col("#ebitda").round().cast(pl.Int64),
    margin_pct=(100 * pl.col("#ebitda") / pl.col("#revenue")).round(1),
    ebitda_chg_pct=(100 * pl.col("#ebitda").pct_change().over("name")).round(1),
)
with pl.Config(tbl_rows=20):
    print(table)

docs.title: Revenue by product and by country
docs.text:
segments(..., hierarchy=PRODUCT), hierarchy=LOCATION

iliad, the French telecom group, reports revenue per business line and per country. One request per hierarchy, then one table.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

template = """
let(#segment = segment_name();
    #revenue = sales_rev_turn(fpt=S, fpo=range(-1S, 0S)) / 1M;)
get(#segment, #revenue)
for(segments('ILD FP Equity', type=reported, hierarchy={hierarchy}, level=1))
"""
frames = []
with BQuery() as bq:
    for hierarchy in ["PRODUCT", "LOCATION"]:
        df = bq.bql(template.format(hierarchy=hierarchy)).combine()
        frames.append(df.with_columns(hierarchy=pl.lit(hierarchy)))
print(
    pl.concat(frames, how="diagonal_relaxed")
    .with_columns(half=pl.col("PERIOD_END_DATE").cast(pl.String))
    .pivot(on="half", index=["hierarchy", "#segment"], values="#revenue")
)

  • iliad reports half-years, hence fpt=S. For a quarterly reporter use fpt=Q and fpo=range(-1Q, 0Q).

docs.title: How much of a high-yield index has fundamentals?
docs.text:
issuerOf vs parent(type=CAST) vs fundamentalticker

Three ways to reach a company from each bond of the Pan-European High Yield index (LP01TREU): the issuer, the CAST parent and fundamentalTicker. For each, the bonds and index weight with a last-twelve-months net debt / EBITDA, and the number of companies they lead to.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
get(id().weights as #weight,
    value(net_debt_to_ebitda(fpt=LTM), issuerOf, mapby=LINEAGE) as #issuerOf,
    value(net_debt_to_ebitda(fpt=LTM), parent(type=CAST), mapby=LINEAGE) as #cast,
    value(net_debt_to_ebitda(fpt=LTM), fundamentalticker, mapby=LINEAGE) as #fundamentalTicker)
for(members('LP01TREU Index'))
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    result = bq.bql(query)
labels = {
    "#issuerOf": "issuerOf",
    "#cast": "parent(type=CAST)",
    "#fundamentalTicker": "fundamentalTicker",
}
weights = result[0].select("ID", "#weight")
rows = []
for name, item in zip(result.names[1:], result.dataframes[1:]):
    covered = item.filter(pl.col(name).is_not_null()).join(weights, on="ID")
    rows.append(
        {
            "mapping": labels[name],
            "bonds": covered.height,
            "pct_bonds": round(100 * covered.height / weights.height, 1),
            "pct_weight": round(covered["#weight"].sum(), 1),
            "companies": covered["SOURCE_ID"].n_unique(),
        }
    )
print(pl.DataFrame(rows))

Output 

shape: (3, 5)
┌───────────────────┬───────┬───────────┬────────────┬───────────┐
│ mapping           ┆ bonds ┆ pct_bonds ┆ pct_weight ┆ companies │
│ ---               ┆ ---   ┆ ---       ┆ ---        ┆ ---       │
│ str               ┆ i64   ┆ f64       ┆ f64        ┆ i64       │
╞═══════════════════╪═══════╪═══════════╪════════════╪═══════════╡
│ issuerOf          ┆ 417   ┆ 55.6      ┆ 56.7       ┆ 194       │
│ parent(type=CAST) ┆ 430   ┆ 57.3      ┆ 57.6       ┆ 188       │
│ fundamentalTicker ┆ 553   ┆ 73.7      ┆ 74.5       ┆ 253       │
└───────────────────┴───────┴───────────┴────────────┴───────────┘

Watch out

The CAST parent can be a shareholder, such as Poste Italiane for Telecom Italia, and a shareholder's leverage is not the bond's.

Notes

  • fundamentalTicker finds a leverage figure for about three bonds in four, the other two mappings for a little over half. It skips financing vehicles without accounts, and it reaches companies that issue through a vehicle.
  • companies counts the companies with a figure. Over the whole index, fundamentalTicker leads to fewer companies than issuerOf, because it puts the vehicles of one group under one company. More of those companies have figures, though.
  • id().weights is the index weight in percent; the weights add up to 100.
  • The three items are used one by one here, because each has its own SOURCE_ID and PERIOD_END_DATE.

docs.title: Median leverage per sector
docs.text:
median(group(..., classification_name(BCLASS, 3)))

Median net debt / EBITDA per Bloomberg (BCLASS) sector, over the companies behind the Pan-European High Yield index. The query runs twice, once over the index's issuers (issuerOf) and once over fundamentalTicker.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

template = """
let(#sector = classification_name(BCLASS, 3);
    #lev = group(net_debt_to_ebitda(fpt=LTM), #sector);)
get(count(#lev) as #n, median(#lev) as #median)
for({universe}(members('LP01TREU Index')))
preferences(dropCols=['ORIG_IDS', 'AS_OF_DATE', 'REVISION_DATE', 'PERIOD_END_DATE'])
"""
tables = []
with BQuery() as bq:
    for universe in ["issuerOf", "fundamentalTicker"]:
        df = bq.bql(template.format(universe=universe)).combine(on="ID")
        tables.append(
            df.select(
                sector=pl.col("ID").replace({"NullGroup": "(no BCLASS sector)"}),
                n=pl.col("#n"),
                median=pl.col("#median").round(1),
            )
        )
table = (
    tables[0]
    .join(tables[1], on="sector", how="full", coalesce=True, suffix="_ft")
    .sort("n_ft", descending=True, nulls_last=True)
)
with pl.Config(tbl_rows=30):
    print(table)

Output
