  • Join on ID, the group's name. The group of companies without a sector has ID NullGroup and a null #SECTOR, and combine() does not match null keys.
  • Leverage of banks and other financials means something else; read those rows with care.

Notes

  • n is the number of companies with a figure, median the median net debt / EBITDA. Columns ending in _ft are for fundamentalTicker.
  • fundamentalTicker gives more companies with a figure in most sectors. Some of the companies it chooses have no BCLASS sector of their own; they end up in (no BCLASS sector).
  • For an index-weighted figure, Bloomberg's announcement averages over the bonds: wavg(group(#x, #sector), group(weights, #sector)) with #x = value(<field>, fundamentalticker, mapby=LINEAGE) over members(...). An average of ratios moves a lot with a few companies whose EBITDA is near zero or negative, so check the inputs.

docs.title: Bloomberg Intelligence sector template
docs.text:
BSRCH: bsrch("BI:TPD", {"BIKEY": ...})

Bloomberg Intelligence (BI) publishes sector figures as dashboards. Each one has a BIKEY, the key in the =@BSRCH("BI:TPD","BIKEY=...") formula it exports to Excel. bsrch() gets the same grid. This one has net leverage and spread per turn of leverage by rating.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

with BQuery() as bq:
    grid = bq.bsrch(
        "BI:TPD", overrides={"BIKEY": "DKOCVGXJVU8II8M90W8JSQEKR", "LIMIT": 20000}
    )
quarters = [c for c in grid.columns if c[:2].isdigit()]
tidy = grid.unpivot(
    index=["Main_Category_Custom_Name", "Category"], on=quarters, variable_name="quarter"
).with_columns(pl.col("quarter").str.to_date("%m/%d/%Y"))
latest = tidy["quarter"].max()
print(f"{len(quarters)} quarters, the latest {latest}")
print(
    tidy.filter(
        pl.col("quarter") == latest,
        pl.col("Main_Category_Custom_Name").str.contains("by Rating|Spread Per Turn"),
        pl.col("Category").is_in(["BB", "B", "CCC"]),
    )
    .with_columns(
        rating=pl.col("Category").cast(pl.Enum(["BB", "B", "CCC"])),
        metric=pl.when(pl.col("Main_Category_Custom_Name").str.starts_with("Spread"))
        .then(pl.lit("spread_per_turn_bp"))
        .otherwise(pl.lit("net_leverage")),
        value=pl.col("value").round(1),
    )
    .pivot(on="metric", index="rating", values="value")
    .sort("rating")
)

Output 

3 quarters, the latest 2025-06-30
shape: (3, 3)
┌────────┬──────────────┬────────────────────┐
│ rating ┆ net_leverage ┆ spread_per_turn_bp │
│ ---    ┆ ---          ┆ ---                │
│ enum   ┆ f64          ┆ f64                │
╞════════╪══════════════╪════════════════════╡
│ BB     ┆ 2.8          ┆ 73.7               │
│ B      ┆ 4.3          ┆ 77.9               │
│ CCC    ┆ 7.1          ┆ 165.0              │
└────────┴──────────────┴────────────────────┘

Watch out

The grid has the columns of the saved dashboard. Check the latest quarter before you use the numbers, and use the BIKEY of your own dashboard for other sectors or fields.

Notes

  • The grid has a column per quarter with the date as MM/DD/YYYY text; unpivot and str.to_date make it a tidy table.
  • LIMIT set high avoids a "reached internal limit" warning; the grid is the same.
  • See BSRCH for overrides and column types.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
What surprised us while writing these recipes.

Symptom Cause Fix Leverage of a bond's issuer is missing The issuer is a financing vehicle without accounts fundamentalticker(...) as universe, or value(<field>, fundamentalticker, mapby=LINEAGE) Companies show different PERIOD_END_DATEs for the "same" quarter fpo=0 is each company's latest report, not a calendar quarter Compare PERIOD_END_DATE; or use fpr=2026Q3 for one calendar quarter (null where not yet reported) fill=PREV does not fill the missing quarter It does not carry a value into a period the company has not reported Use the latest reported period (fpo=0) and show its date fpt=LTM is null, but the company reports quarters (VMED O2 UK Holdings) Bloomberg has no LTM figure for that company Add up the last four quarters: sum(ebitda(fpt=Q, fpo=range(-3Q, 0Q))) A group with a null key is split over two rows combine() does not match null keys such as the null #SECTOR of NullGroup combine(on="ID"); the group's ID is never null A company appears on two rows after combine() Fields carry different REVISION_DATEs, or grouped items different PERIOD_END_DATEs preferences(dropCols=['AS_OF_DATE', 'REVISION_DATE']), plus 'PERIOD_END_DATE' for groups count(group(id)) over fundamentalticker(members(...)) returns the number of bonds It counts the bonds that went in (750 for LP01TREU), not the companies Count the rows of get(name) for(fundamentalticker(...)) segments(..., hierarchy=GEOGRAPHY) fails The hierarchy is called LOCATION hierarchy=LOCATION Segment revenue of a bank is null sales_rev_turn is not filled for bank segments Use group figures, or a field the bank reports per segment Fundamentals in the reporting currency although you asked for EUR with(ccy=EUR) is ignored without an error with(currency=EUR) or field(currency=EUR); check CURRENCY

docs.title: Market History with BDH
docs.text:
BQL screens a universe and computes. BDH, bq.bdh() here and =BDH() in Excel, does something simpler: it returns the history of a few fields for a list of securities. The query is short, so the work is in the options.

The options decide which dates you get (days, Fridays, month-ends, fiscal years) and what happens on a day when one market is closed and another is open. Get them wrong and you get a frame that looks right but has gaps, half-empty rows or misaligned dates.

Data on this page

This page uses the series a credit desk pulls every week: bond index spreads, CDS indices, fund NAVs and flows, the cost of hedging dollars into euros, government yields, fiscal-year fundamentals and price candles.

The outputs below are live data as of 2026-11-17 and will differ when you run the queries. The recipes with fixed dates change only when Bloomberg revises its data. Before you adapt a query, read the Pitfalls.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text:
bdh() returns a long frame with a security column, a date column and one column per field. pivot(on="security", ...) makes one column per security.

By taskOptions You want Use One row per Weekly, monthly or yearly closes options={"periodicitySelection": "WEEKLY"}, MONTHLY, YEARLY security and period Markets with different holidays on the same dates "nonTradingDayFillOption": "NON_TRADING_WEEKDAYS", "nonTradingDayFillMethod": "PREVIOUS_VALUE" security and weekday A fund's NAV, assets and flows FUND_NET_ASSET_VAL, FUND_TOTAL_ASSETS, FUND_CLASS_ASSETS, FUND_FLOW fund and date A CDS index against its constituents CDS_INDEX_INTRINSIC_VALUE, CDS_INDEX_INTRINSIC_BASIS_VALUE index and date FX, hedging cost and yields side by side several securities, PX_LAST, then pivot(on="security") date Fundamentals per fiscal year "periodicitySelection": "YEARLY", "periodicityAdjustment": "FISCAL" company and fiscal year Values in another currency "currency": "USD" Open, high, low and close PX_OPEN, PX_HIGH, PX_LOW, PX_LAST security and day, week or month

The options go in one dict, options={...}. The values are strings.

Option Values Default Effect periodicitySelection DAILY, WEEKLY, MONTHLY, QUARTERLY, SEMI_ANNUALLY, YEARLY DAILY One row per period periodicityAdjustment CALENDAR, ACTUAL, FISCAL calendar periods CALENDAR: weeks end on Friday, months on the last business day. ACTUAL: periods end on end_date, so weeks end on its weekday. FISCAL: on each company's fiscal period end nonTradingDayFillOption ACTIVE_DAYS_ONLY, NON_TRADING_WEEKDAYS, ALL_CALENDAR_DAYS ACTIVE_DAYS_ONLY Which dates get a row nonTradingDayFillMethod PREVIOUS_VALUE, NIL_VALUE PREVIOUS_VALUE What an added date holds currency EUR, USD, SEK, ... the security's own Converts prices, fund assets and fundamentals

start_date and end_date take a date or a string, "2026-04-01" or "20260401".

docs.title: High-yield spreads, week by week
docs.text:
periodicitySelection=WEEKLY, INDEX_OAS_TSY_BP

Friday OAS of four Bloomberg bond indices for the last twelve weeks: US High Yield (LF98TRUU), its Industrials sector (I00423), Pan-European High Yield (LP01TREU) and Contingent Capital EUR (I30904EU). In basis points.

from datetime import date, timedelta

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

indices = {
    "LF98TRUU Index": "us_hy",
    "I00423 Index": "us_hy_industrials",
    "LP01TREU Index": "euro_hy",
    "I30904EU Index": "eur_coco",
}
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bdh(
        list(indices),
        ["INDEX_OAS_TSY_BP"],
        start_date=date.today() - timedelta(weeks=12),
        end_date=date.today(),
        options={"periodicitySelection": "WEEKLY"},
    )
oas = df.with_columns(pl.col("security").replace_strict(indices)).pivot(
    on="security", index="date", values="INDEX_OAS_TSY_BP"
)
with pl.Config(tbl_rows=20):
    print(oas.select("date", pl.col(list(indices.values())).round().cast(pl.Int64)))

Output

Watch out

  • WEEKLY gives each week's Friday close. The current week is not there until it is complete. For the latest close, add a daily request or use BQL's per=W, as in Index yield and spread, week by week.
  • "periodicityAdjustment": "ACTUAL" ends each week on the weekday of end_date. Run it on a Wednesday and you get Wednesday closes.

Notes

  • INDEX_OAS_TSY_BP is the OAS in basis points, and INDEX_OAS_TSY is the same number in percent. INDEX_Z_SPREAD_BP is the Z-spread.
  • Field ids work as well as mnemonics: "BX218" is INDEX_OAS_TSY_BP and "BX326" is INDEX_Z_SPREAD_BP. The column is named as you asked, so BX218. Look fields up with FLDS <GO>.
  • replace_strict turns tickers into short names before the pivot. It raises an error for a ticker that is missing from the dict, so a typo does not go unnoticed.

docs.title: Three markets, one calendar
docs.text:
nonTradingDayFillOption, nonTradingDayFillMethod

The S&P 500, Euro Stoxx 50 and OMX Stockholm 30 around Easter 2026. On Good Friday, 3 April, all three were closed. On Easter Monday, 6 April, only New York traded. The recipe asks for every weekday, carries the last close into holidays and lists the markets that were closed.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

markets = ["SPX Index", "SX5E Index", "OMX Index"]
every_weekday = {
    "nonTradingDayFillOption": "NON_TRADING_WEEKDAYS",
    "nonTradingDayFillMethod": "PREVIOUS_VALUE",
}
with BQuery() as bq:
    traded = bq.bdh(markets, "PX_LAST", "2026-04-01", "2026-04-08")
    filled = bq.bdh(
        markets, "PX_LAST", "2026-04-01", "2026-04-08", options=every_weekday
    )
closed = (
    filled.join(traded, on=["security", "date"], how="anti")
    .group_by("date")
    .agg(closed=pl.col("security").str.replace(" Index", "").sort().str.join(", "))
)
print(
    filled.pivot(on="security", index="date", values="PX_LAST")
    .join(closed, on="date", how="left")
    .sort("date")
    .select("date", pl.col("date").dt.strftime("%a").alias("day"), *markets, "closed")
)

Output

┌────────────┬─────┬───────────┬────────────┬───────────┬────────────────┐
│ date       ┆ day ┆ SPX Index ┆ SX5E Index ┆ OMX Index ┆ closed         │

│ date       ┆ str ┆ f64       ┆ f64        ┆ f64       ┆ str            │

│ 2026-04-01 ┆ Wed ┆ 6575.32   ┆ 5732.71    ┆ 3006.37   ┆ null           │
│ 2026-04-02 ┆ Thu ┆ 6582.69   ┆ 5692.86    ┆ 2965.688  ┆ null           │
│ 2026-04-03 ┆ Fri ┆ 6582.69   ┆ 5692.86    ┆ 2965.688  ┆ OMX, SPX, SX5E │
│ 2026-04-06 ┆ Mon ┆ 6611.83   ┆ 5692.86    ┆ 2965.688  ┆ OMX, SX5E      │
│ 2026-04-07 ┆ Tue ┆ 6616.85   ┆ 5633.22    ┆ 2967.917  ┆ null           │
│ 2026-04-08 ┆ Wed ┆ 6782.81   ┆ 5913.37    ┆ 3094.161  ┆ null           │

Watch out

  • Without options (traded) each security keeps its own trading days. Good Friday has no row at all, and Easter Monday has one only for the S&P 500. After a pivot Europe is null on Easter Monday. Computed per security, Europe's return on Tuesday covers Thursday to Tuesday, and New York's only Monday to Tuesday.
  • nonTradingDayFillMethod alone changes nothing. The default nonTradingDayFillOption, ACTIVE_DAYS_ONLY, adds no days to fill.

Notes

  • NON_TRADING_WEEKDAYS gives a row for every Monday to Friday. PREVIOUS_VALUE repeats the last close on the added days, so the return on a holiday is 0.
  • ALL_CALENDAR_DAYS adds Saturdays and Sundays too, which helps when a month ends on a weekend. NIL_VALUE adds the days but leaves them null.
  • The anti join finds the rows that only the fill created. Those are the holidays.

docs.title: Fund NAV, assets and flows
docs.text:
FUND_TOTAL_ASSETS, FUND_FLOW, MONTHLY

Month-end NAV, return and assets of two AT1 funds: the SEB Hybrid Capital Bond Fund (SEBVVGD, a UCITS fund, share class R EUR) and the Invesco USD AT1 CoCo Bond UCITS ETF (AT1 LN). class_flow is Bloomberg's flow into the share class. fund_flow estimates the flow into the whole fund from its assets and the NAV return. Assets and flows are in millions of the fund's currency, EUR and USD.

from datetime import date, timedelta

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bdh(
        ["SEBVVGD SS Equity", "AT1 LN Equity"],
        ["FUND_NET_ASSET_VAL", "FUND_TOTAL_ASSETS", "FUND_FLOW"],
        start_date=date.today() - timedelta(days=200),
        end_date=date.today(),
        options={"periodicitySelection": "MONTHLY"},
    )
growth = pl.col("FUND_NET_ASSET_VAL") / pl.col("FUND_NET_ASSET_VAL").shift()
aum = pl.col("FUND_TOTAL_ASSETS")
table = (
    df.with_columns(
        ret_pct=(100 * (growth - 1)).over("security"),
        fund_flow=(aum - aum.shift() * growth).over("security"),
    )
    .drop_nulls("fund_flow")
    .select(
        fund=pl.col("security").str.split(" ").list.first(),
        month="date",
        nav=pl.col("FUND_NET_ASSET_VAL").round(2),
        ret_pct=pl.col("ret_pct").round(2),
        aum=aum.round(1),
        class_flow=pl.col("FUND_FLOW").round(1),
        fund_flow=pl.col("fund_flow").round(1),
    )
)
with pl.Config(tbl_rows=20):
    print(table)

Output

│ str     ┆ date       ┆ f64    ┆ f64     ┆ f64    ┆ f64        ┆ f64       │

Watch out

  • With MONTHLY, FUND_FLOW is the sum of the month's daily flows. NAV and assets are month-end values. The current month is missing until it ends.
  • PX_LAST of a mutual fund is its NAV. For an ETF it is the exchange price, and PX_LAST / FUND_NET_ASSET_VAL - 1 is the premium to NAV.

Notes

  • FUND_TOTAL_ASSETS is the whole fund, all share classes together. FUND_CLASS_ASSETS is the share class of the ticker you ask for, and FUND_TOTAL_ASSETS_CRNCY gives the currency.
  • Assets are shares times NAV. So the change in assets less the NAV return is the money that came in or went out. Computed with FUND_CLASS_ASSETS, it comes close to Bloomberg's FUND_FLOW. With FUND_TOTAL_ASSETS it is an estimate for the whole fund, because the other share classes earn slightly different returns (other currencies, other fees).
  • A month where class_flow is close to 0 and fund_flow is large means money moved in the fund's other share classes.
  • "currency": "SEK" returns the assets in SEK. Bloomberg converts them.

docs.title: CDS index vs intrinsic: the basis
docs.text:
CDS_INDEX_INTRINSIC_BASIS_VALUE

iTraxx Europe Main and Crossover, 5-year, for the last three weeks. For each index the quoted spread, the intrinsic spread (the index spread implied by the CDS of its constituents) and the basis between them, in basis points.

from datetime import date, timedelta

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

indices = {"ITRXEBE Index": "main", "ITRXEXE Index": "xover"}
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bdh(
        list(indices),
        ["PX_LAST", "CDS_INDEX_INTRINSIC_VALUE", "CDS_INDEX_INTRINSIC_BASIS_VALUE"],
        start_date=date.today() - timedelta(weeks=3),
        end_date=date.today(),
    )
wide = df.select(
    "date",
    index=pl.col("security").replace_strict(indices),
    spread=pl.col("PX_LAST").round(1),
    intrinsic=pl.col("CDS_INDEX_INTRINSIC_VALUE").round(1),
    basis=pl.col("CDS_INDEX_INTRINSIC_BASIS_VALUE"),
).pivot(on="index", index="date", values=["spread", "intrinsic", "basis"])
with pl.Config(tbl_rows=30):
    print(
        wide.select(
            "date",
            "spread_main",
            "intrinsic_main",
            "basis_main",
            "spread_xover",
            "intrinsic_xover",
            "basis_xover",
        )
    )

Output 

shape: (16, 7)

  • For the return of selling protection on Main, use the excess return index ERIXITEU Index.

docs.title: US Treasuries hedged into euros vs Bunds
docs.text:
FXHCEUUS Index, pivot(on="security")

Should a euro investor buy 5-year US Treasuries hedged back into euros, or 5-year Bunds? Month-end EURUSD, the cost of hedging dollars into euros with 3-month forwards, both yields, and the hedged pickup over Bunds. Four securities, one field, one wide frame.

from datetime import date, timedelta

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

names = {
    "EURUSD Curncy": "eurusd",
    "FXHCEUUS Index": "hedge_cost",
    "USGG5YR Index": "ust_5y",
    "GDBR5 Index": "bund_5y",
}
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bdh(
        list(names),
        "PX_LAST",
        start_date=date.today() - timedelta(days=365),
        end_date=date.today(),
        options={"periodicitySelection": "MONTHLY"},
    )
wide = df.with_columns(pl.col("security").replace_strict(names)).pivot(
    on="security", index="date", values="PX_LAST"
)
hedged = pl.col("ust_5y") + pl.col("hedge_cost")
with pl.Config(tbl_rows=20):
    print(
        wide.select(
            "date",
            *names.values(),
            ust_hedged=hedged.round(2),
            pickup_bp=(100 * (hedged - pl.col("bund_5y"))).round(),
        )
    )

Output

│ date       ┆ f64    ┆ f64        ┆ f64    ┆ f64     ┆ f64        ┆ f64       │

│ 2026-03-31 ┆ 1.1553 ┆ -1.6378    ┆ 3.9427 ┆ 2.727   ┆ 2.3        ┆ -42.0     │

Watch out

FXHCEUUS (Bloomberg EURUSD 3 Month Hedging Cost) is the annualised return, in percent, of selling dollars three months forward for euros. It is negative when hedging costs a euro investor money, so add it to the dollar yield. It follows the forward points. On 13 November 2026, EURUSD at 1.1023 and 3-month points of 44.77 (EUR3M Curncy) came to about -1.6% a year, and the index stood at -1.59.

Notes

  • FXHCUSEU is the other side: a dollar investor hedging euros earns about the same amount.
  • The hedge is rolled every three months. ust_hedged holds only while the gap between dollar and euro short rates stays where it is.
  • Holidays differ between New York, Frankfurt and the FX market. Month-ends hide that. For daily data, add the options from Three markets, one calendar.
  • To get the hedge cost known on each trade date, sort both frames by date and use trades.join_asof(hedge, on="date"). Each trade gets the last value on or before its date.

docs.title: Fiscal-year leverage
docs.text:
YEARLY, periodicityAdjustment=FISCAL, currency

Reported and adjusted EBITDA, net debt and net leverage for each fiscal year, for three companies whose years end in different months: IBM (December), Vodafone (March) and Microsoft (June). In USD billions.

from datetime import date

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bdh(
        ["IBM US Equity", "VOD LN Equity", "MSFT US Equity"],
        ["TRAIL_12M_EBITDA", "EBITDA_ADJUSTED", "NET_DEBT"],
        start_date=date(date.today().year - 4, 1, 1),
        end_date=date.today(),
        options={
            "periodicitySelection": "YEARLY",
            "periodicityAdjustment": "FISCAL",
            "currency": "USD",
        },
    )
with pl.Config(tbl_rows=20):
    print(
        df.select(
            company=pl.col("security").str.split(" ").list.first(),
            fiscal_year_end="date",
            ebitda=(pl.col("TRAIL_12M_EBITDA") / 1000).round(1),
            ebitda_adj=(pl.col("EBITDA_ADJUSTED") / 1000).round(1),
            net_debt=(pl.col("NET_DEBT") / 1000).round(1),
            leverage=(pl.col("NET_DEBT") / pl.col("EBITDA_ADJUSTED")).round(1),
        )
    )

Output

│ IBM     ┆ 2023-12-31      ┆ 13.9   ┆ 14.3       ┆ 46.5     ┆ 3.2      │
│ IBM     ┆ 2024-12-31      ┆ 14.0   ┆ 18.2       ┆ 43.8     ┆ 2.4      │
│ IBM     ┆ 2025-12-31      ┆ 16.9   ┆ 17.6       ┆ 50.2     ┆ 2.9      │
│ VOD     ┆ 2022-03-31      ┆ 18.3   ┆ 18.7       ┆ 60.6     ┆ 3.2      │
│ VOD     ┆ 2023-03-31      ┆ 25.3   ┆ 16.2       ┆ 51.8     ┆ 3.2      │

│ MSFT    ┆ 2022-06-30      ┆ 100.3  ┆ 100.3      ┆ -26.4    ┆ -0.3     │
│ MSFT    ┆ 2023-06-30      ┆ 105.3  ┆ 106.4      ┆ -31.8    ┆ -0.3     │
│ MSFT    ┆ 2024-06-30      ┆ 135.3  ┆ 135.3      ┆ 22.3     ┆ 0.2      │

Watch out

  • "periodicityAdjustment": "FISCAL" puts every field on the company's fiscal year end. Without it, TRAIL_12M_EBITDA lands on the last trading day of each calendar year and NET_DEBT on the fiscal year end. When the two dates differ, as they do every year for Vodafone and Microsoft, the year has two rows, each half null.
  • CALENDAR does not calendarise the figures; it only relabels them. Microsoft's fiscal year to June 2023 and Vodafone's to March 2023 both come back dated 2022-12-30. Keep FISCAL and the real period end.
  • Vodafone reports in EUR and "currency": "USD" converts. EBITDA is converted at the average rate of the year and net debt at the rate at year end: about 1.16 and 1.11 USD per EUR for fiscal 2022. So leverage in USD can differ from leverage in the reporting currency.

Notes

  • TRAIL_12M_EBITDA is EBITDA as reported. EBITDA_ADJUSTED takes out one-off items. Vodafone's fiscal 2023 shows the difference: 25.3 reported, 16.2 adjusted.
  • Amounts are in millions; the recipe divides by 1,000. Negative net debt is net cash.
  • For period offsets, segments, adjusted figures and estimates in BQL, see Company Fundamentals.

docs.title: Weekly candles
docs.text:
PX_OPEN, PX_HIGH, PX_LOW, WEEKLY

Weekly open, high, low and close of the S&P 500 for the last eight weeks, with the week's range and change in percent.

from datetime import date, timedelta

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bdh(
        "SPX Index",
        ["PX_OPEN", "PX_HIGH", "PX_LOW", "PX_LAST"],
        start_date=date.today() - timedelta(weeks=8),
        end_date=date.today(),
        options={"periodicitySelection": "WEEKLY"},
    )
print(
    df.select(
        week_ending="date",
        open="PX_OPEN",
        high="PX_HIGH",
        low="PX_LOW",
        close="PX_LAST",
        range_pct=(
            100 * (pl.col("PX_HIGH") - pl.col("PX_LOW")) / pl.col("PX_LAST")
        ).round(1),
        chg_pct=(100 * pl.col("PX_LAST").pct_change()).round(1),
    )
)

Output

  • A start date in the middle of a week still gives the whole first week. The current week appears once it is complete.
  • To check the data, test low <= min(open, close) and max(open, close) <= high on each row.
  • For a chart, plotly's go.Candlestick(x=..., open=..., high=..., low=..., close=...) takes these columns as they are.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
What surprised us while writing these recipes.

Symptom Cause Fix Weekly rows on Wednesdays "periodicityAdjustment": "ACTUAL" ends weeks on the weekday of end_date Leave it out, or CALENDAR, for Friday closes The current week or month is missing Weekly and monthly BDH return complete periods only Add a daily request, or use BQL with per=W Nulls after a pivot, holidays missing Each security keeps its own trading days NON_TRADING_WEEKDAYS with PREVIOUS_VALUE "nonTradingDayFillMethod": "PREVIOUS_VALUE" changes nothing The default fill option adds no days Add "nonTradingDayFillOption": "NON_TRADING_WEEKDAYS" or ALL_CALENDAR_DAYS Two rows per year, each half null YEARLY without FISCAL: trailing fields on calendar year ends, reported fields on fiscal year ends "periodicityAdjustment": "FISCAL" Microsoft's fiscal 2023 dated 2022-12-30 CALENDAR relabels fiscal years FISCAL A column named BX218 Field ids are accepted, and the column keeps the name you asked for Use the mnemonic, INDEX_OAS_TSY_BP, or rename Index OAS 100 times smaller than in BQL INDEX_OAS_TSY is in percent INDEX_OAS_TSY_BP The CDS basis has the opposite sign to its description CDS_INDEX_INTRINSIC_BASIS_VALUE is quoted minus intrinsic Read positive as "index wider than its constituents" Today's intrinsic spread is null During the day only the quoted spread is there drop_nulls(), or end yesterday A CDS index jumps around 20 March or 20 September The generic ticker rolled to a new series Mark the roll dates, or use the series' own ticker FUND_FLOW is 0 while the fund's assets fell FUND_FLOW is for one share class, FUND_TOTAL_ASSETS for all of them Compare with FUND_CLASS_ASSETS, or estimate the fund's flows Leverage in USD differs from leverage in EUR EBITDA converts at the year's average rate, net debt at the year-end rate Compute leverage in the reporting currency The hedged yield is too high FXHCEUUS is negative when hedging costs money Add it to the yield; do not subtract it

Related

See also FLDS <GO> for field mnemonics and ids, and HP <GO> for one security's history on the Terminal. For how bdh() works, see BDH.

docs.title: New Issues
docs.text:
BQL can see bonds that are announced but not yet priced, in line with SRCH <GO> and PREL <GO>. The universe covers deals that are announced and unpriced, or that priced within the last calendar day.

Each deal's progress is in LATST_STATS_FOR_MOST_RECENT_DEAL:

  1. Mandate
  2. Guidance
  3. IPT
  4. New Deal

Two switches are needed

bondsUniv(INCLUDEPRELIMINARYSECURITIES='Y') adds preliminary securities to the universe, and PRELIMINARY_SECURITY=='Y' keeps only those. Without the filter you get the whole active bond universe.

Data on this page

The outputs below are live data as of 2026-11-17 and will differ when you run the queries.

docs.title: New AT1 / RT1 deals in USD, EUR, GBP
docs.text:
INCLUDEPRELIMINARYSECURITIES, issuance_pricing, as #alias

Bank AT1s and insurance RT1s currently in the pipeline, with deal status, marketed tenor and initial price talk.

from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
for(filter(bondsUniv(INCLUDEPRELIMINARYSECURITIES='Y'),
        PRELIMINARY_SECURITY=='Y' and
        crncy() in ['USD', 'EUR', 'GBP'] and
        (basel_iii_designation() == 'Additional Tier 1' or
         solvency_ii_designation() == 'Restricted Tier 1')))
get(name, LATST_STATS_FOR_MOST_RECENT_DEAL, marketing_tenor,
    issuance_pricing as #IPT)
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine(on="ID")
print(df)

Output

┌───────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────┬──────┬──────────────┐
│ ID            ┆ name          ┆ LATST_STATS_FOR_MOST_RECENT_DEAL ┆ marketing_tenor ┆ #IPT ┆ PRICING_TYPE │
│ ---           ┆ ---           ┆ ---                              ┆ ---             ┆ ---  ┆ ---          │
│ str           ┆ str           ┆ str                              ┆ str             ┆ f64  ┆ str          │

Notes

  • as #IPT renames a column without a let() block.
  • #IPT and PRICING_TYPE stay null until the deal reaches the IPT stage. Until the deal prices, the coupon in name is often a placeholder 0.
  • issuance_pricing returns two columns (the value and PRICING_TYPE), so the result holds four DataFrames, and combine(on="ID") joins them into one row per bond.

│ str      ┆ i64   │
╞══════════╪═══════╡
│ JPY      ┆ 103   │
│ CNY      ┆ 98    │
│ USD      ┆ 49    │
│ EUR      ┆ 30    │
│ IDR      ┆ 28    │
│ MYR      ┆ 28    │
└──────────┴───────┘

Notes

  • With group(...), the ID column holds the group key, not a security.
  • The result also has ORIG_IDS:* columns, which are filled only when a group has one member. The select() drops them.

Related

See also BQLX <GO>. The Bloomberg Excel templates "BQL for Primary Markets" and "BQL for Issuance Pricing Analysis" cover the same workflows.

docs.title: Spread Statistics
docs.text:
How wide are spreads for each rating? How much more does an AT1 pay than a bond with the same rating? Is the market wider than last month? And what spread does a bond have at the price you are about to pay?

BQL answers the first three for a whole index in one request: it groups the bonds' spreads and sends back only the statistics. The last one is the YAS calculator (YAS <GO>), which BQL runs at any price and workout you give it.

Data on this page

Spreads are in basis points, yields in percent. The outputs below are live data as of 2026-11-17 and will differ when you run the queries. Before you adapt a query, read the Pitfalls.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text:
By taskSpread types You want Use One row per Count, median and quartiles of spreads per rating count(), median(), quantile(..., 0.75) of group(spread(...), by=[bb_composite(), ...]) group The same statistics month by month spread(dates=range(-6M, 0D), per=M), grouped by year() and month() of its DATE group and month One number per day for all bonds of an index avg(group(#s, by=#s().DATE)) day An index's own yield and spread yield(yield_type=YTW, universe_type=PROJECTED), spread(spread_type=OAS_SOVEREIGN, universe_type=RETURNS) date Spread or yield at your price, to call, maturity or a date spread(price=..., workout=TO_NEXT_CALL), TO_MATURITY, TO_WORST, TO_CUSTOM bond Discount margin of a floating rate note discount_margin(price=...) bond spread_type= Spread Works for Z (the default) Z-spread: constant spread over the swap zero curve bonds, indices OAS option-adjusted spread bonds G, I, ASW over government yields, over swap rates, asset swap bonds OAS_SOVEREIGN, OAS_SWAP index OAS over government or swap curve indices

Name the spread type

spread() without spread_type is the Z-spread, not the OAS, so every recipe names the type.

docs.title: OAS by rating: AT1 vs other bonds
docs.text:
median(), quantile(), group(..., by=[bb_composite(), ...])

Count, median and upper quartile OAS per rating from BBB+ to BB-, for AT1s (CoCos) and for all other bonds of three European indices: Bloomberg Contingent Capital Western Europe (I31095), Pan-European High Yield (LP01STAT) and Pan-European Aggregate Corporate (LP05STAT).

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
let(#is_coco = if(capital_contingent_security(), true, false);
    #oas = group(spread(spread_type=OAS), by=[bb_composite(), #is_coco]);)
get(count(#oas) as #n, median(#oas) as #median, quantile(#oas, 0.75) as #q3)
for(filter(members(['I31095 Index', 'LP01STAT Index', 'LP05STAT Index']),
           bb_composite() in ['BBB+', 'BBB', 'BBB-', 'BB+', 'BB', 'BB-']))
preferences(dropCols=['ORIG_IDS'])
"""
ratings = pl.Enum(["BBB+", "BBB", "BBB-", "BB+", "BB", "BB-"])
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine()
stats = df.select(
    rating=pl.col("BB_COMPOSITE()").cast(ratings),
    at1="#IS_COCO",
    n="#n",
    median=pl.col("#median").round().cast(pl.Int64),
    q3=pl.col("#q3").round().cast(pl.Int64),
)
print(
    stats.filter(~pl.col("at1"))
    .drop("at1")
    .join(stats.filter(pl.col("at1")).drop("at1"), on="rating", suffix="_at1")
    .with_columns(premium=pl.col("median_at1") - pl.col("median"))
    .sort("rating")
)

Output 

shape: (6, 8)
┌────────┬──────┬────────┬─────┬───────┬────────────┬────────┬─────────┐
│ rating ┆ n    ┆ median ┆ q3  ┆ n_at1 ┆ median_at1 ┆ q3_at1 ┆ premium │
│ ---    ┆ ---  ┆ ---    ┆ --- ┆ ---   ┆ ---        ┆ ---    ┆ ---     │
│ enum   ┆ i64  ┆ i64    ┆ i64 ┆ i64   ┆ i64        ┆ i64    ┆ i64     │
╞════════╪══════╪════════╪═════╪═══════╪════════════╪════════╪═════════╡
│ BBB+   ┆ 1043 ┆ 96     ┆ 131 ┆ 3     ┆ 228        ┆ 256    ┆ 132     │
│ BBB    ┆ 695  ┆ 92     ┆ 122 ┆ 21    ┆ 229        ┆ 269    ┆ 137     │
│ BBB-   ┆ 385  ┆ 107    ┆ 147 ┆ 92    ┆ 259        ┆ 287    ┆ 152     │
│ BB+    ┆ 172  ┆ 129    ┆ 170 ┆ 44    ┆ 257        ┆ 288    ┆ 128     │
│ BB     ┆ 106  ┆ 149    ┆ 202 ┆ 37    ┆ 285        ┆ 325    ┆ 136     │
│ BB-    ┆ 102  ┆ 161    ┆ 247 ┆ 5     ┆ 252        ┆ 270    ┆ 91      │
└────────┴──────┴────────┴─────┴───────┴────────────┴────────┴─────────┘

Watch out

if(capital_contingent_security(), true, false) matters. The flag itself is null for most bonds that are not CoCos, their groups get a null key, and combine() cannot join them (see Pitfalls).

Notes

  • n is the number of bonds, median and q3 the 50th and 75th percentile OAS of the group. Columns ending in _at1 are the AT1s. premium is how much wider the median AT1 is than the median bond of the same rating.
  • A group column is named after its expression in upper case: BB_COMPOSITE(), #IS_COCO. The ID column holds the whole group key, such as BB+:true.
  • bb_composite() is today's rating. For a box plot, add quantile(#oas, 0.25) for the box and quantile(#oas, 0.05), quantile(#oas, 0.95) for the whiskers.
  • For the AT1 premium per rating over ten years, with charts, see the AT1 vs Credits OAS per Rating example.

docs.title: Median OAS by rating, month by month
docs.text:
per=M, month(), year()

Median OAS at the last six month-ends and today, for the ratings around the line between investment grade and high yield, in the Pan-European High Yield and Aggregate Corporate indices. crossover is BB+ minus BBB-: the extra spread for one notch below investment grade.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
let(#oas = spread(spread_type=OAS, dates=range(-6M, 0D), per=M, fill=PREV);
    #year = year(#oas().DATE);
    #month = month(#oas().DATE);
    #median = median(group(#oas, by=[bb_composite(), #year, #month]));)
get(#median)
for(filter(members(['LP01STAT Index', 'LP05STAT Index']),
           bb_composite() in ['BBB', 'BBB-', 'BB+', 'BB']))
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine()
print(
    df.drop_nulls("DATE")
    .pivot(on="BB_COMPOSITE()", index="DATE", values="#median")
    .sort("DATE")
    .select(
        "DATE",
        pl.col("BBB", "BBB-", "BB+", "BB").round(),
        crossover=(pl.col("BB+") - pl.col("BBB-")).round(),
    )
)

Output 

shape: (7, 6)
┌────────────┬──────┬───────┬───────┬───────┬───────────┐
│ DATE       ┆ BBB  ┆ BBB-  ┆ BB+   ┆ BB    ┆ crossover │
│ ---        ┆ ---  ┆ ---   ┆ ---   ┆ ---   ┆ ---       │
│ date       ┆ f64  ┆ f64   ┆ f64   ┆ f64   ┆ f64       │
╞════════════╪══════╪═══════╪═══════╪═══════╪═══════════╡
│ 2026-05-29 ┆ 81.0 ┆ 98.0  ┆ 120.0 ┆ 151.0 ┆ 22.0      │
│ 2026-06-30 ┆ 81.0 ┆ 95.0  ┆ 121.0 ┆ 146.0 ┆ 25.0      │
│ 2026-07-31 ┆ 78.0 ┆ 91.0  ┆ 114.0 ┆ 129.0 ┆ 23.0      │
│ 2026-08-31 ┆ 77.0 ┆ 90.0  ┆ 105.0 ┆ 118.0 ┆ 15.0      │
│ 2026-09-30 ┆ 82.0 ┆ 94.0  ┆ 128.0 ┆ 149.0 ┆ 33.0      │
│ 2026-10-30 ┆ 93.0 ┆ 106.0 ┆ 145.0 ┆ 172.0 ┆ 39.0      │
│ 2026-11-17 ┆ 92.0 ┆ 107.0 ┆ 129.0 ┆ 149.0 ┆ 21.0      │
└────────────┴──────┴───────┴───────┴───────┴───────────┘

Watch out

  • per=M gives the last business day of each month and the latest close. frq=M instead steps back from today in whole months: run it on the 17th and every row is the 17th.
  • members() is today's index. Bonds that have left the index are missing from the history, and new issues count only from their issue date. Add count(group(...)) to see how many bonds each median uses.

Notes

  • year() and month() of #oas().DATE put the period into the group key, so each rating gets one median per month.
  • A bond without any spread history falls into a group whose date is null. drop_nulls("DATE") removes that row.
  • fill=PREV carries the last spread forward over days without a price.
  • For AT1 vs other bonds per rating since 2014, see the AT1 vs Credits OAS per Rating example.

docs.title: Daily average Z-spread of index members
docs.text:
avg(group(#s, by=#s().DATE))

The average and median Z-spread of the bonds in the Bloomberg European Banks CoCo Tier 1 index (I31415), for each business day of the last two weeks, with the daily change of the average.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
let(#z = spread(spread_type=Z, dates=range(-14D, 0D));
    #day = #z().DATE;
    #avg = avg(group(#z, by=#day));
    #median = median(group(#z, by=#day));
    #n = count(group(#z, by=#day));)
get(#avg, #median, #n)
for(members('I31415 Index'))
preferences(dropCols=['ORIG_IDS'])
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine()
print(
    df.filter(pl.col("#n") > 0)
    .sort("DATE")
    .select(
        "DATE",
        bonds="#n",
        avg=pl.col("#avg").round(1),
        median=pl.col("#median").round(1),
        change=pl.col("#avg").diff().round(1),
    )
)

Output 

shape: (10, 5)
┌────────────┬───────┬───────┬────────┬────────┐
│ DATE       ┆ bonds ┆ avg   ┆ median ┆ change │
│ ---        ┆ ---   ┆ ---   ┆ ---    ┆ ---    │
│ date       ┆ i64   ┆ f64   ┆ f64    ┆ f64    │
╞════════════╪═══════╪═══════╪════════╪════════╡
│ 2026-11-03 ┆ 232   ┆ 291.0 ┆ 284.6  ┆ null   │
│ 2026-11-04 ┆ 232   ┆ 287.0 ┆ 282.4  ┆ -4.0   │
│ 2026-11-05 ┆ 234   ┆ 288.1 ┆ 285.5  ┆ 1.1    │
│ 2026-11-06 ┆ 234   ┆ 288.8 ┆ 284.8  ┆ 0.7    │
│ 2026-11-09 ┆ 225   ┆ 274.2 ┆ 270.7  ┆ -14.6  │
│ 2026-11-10 ┆ 234   ┆ 263.1 ┆ 259.0  ┆ -11.1  │
│ 2026-11-11 ┆ 139   ┆ 261.1 ┆ 258.9  ┆ -2.0   │
│ 2026-11-12 ┆ 235   ┆ 259.4 ┆ 255.1  ┆ -1.7   │
│ 2026-11-13 ┆ 235   ┆ 265.0 ┆ 260.0  ┆ 5.6    │
│ 2026-11-16 ┆ 235   ┆ 270.5 ┆ 264.8  ┆ 5.4    │
└────────────┴───────┴───────┴────────┴────────┘

Watch out

  • bonds is the number of bonds with a spread that day. Weekends, and today until the close is stored, have none and are dropped. On a holiday in one market fewer bonds are priced, and the average moves because the set of bonds changed; check bonds before you read change as a market move.
  • preferences(dropCols=['ORIG_IDS']) is needed here: ORIG_IDS is null in every row, and the three items would not join.

Notes

  • #z().DATE is the date of each spread. Grouping by it gives one value per day for all bonds together.
  • This is an equal-weighted average. The index's own spread is weighted by market value; the next recipe gets it.

docs.title: Index yield and spread, week by week
docs.text:
universe_type, per=W

Yield to worst and OAS of the Bloomberg Contingent Capital EUR index (I30904EU) at each Friday close for the last eight weeks. rates is the yield minus the spread: what is left once the credit spread is taken out, mostly the government bond yield. spread_pct is the spread's share of the yield, in percent.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
let(#ytw = yield(yield_type=YTW, universe_type=PROJECTED);
    #oas = spread(spread_type=OAS_SOVEREIGN, universe_type=RETURNS);)
get(#ytw, #oas)
for(['I30904EU Index'])
with(dates=range(-8W, 0D), per=W, fill=PREV)
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine()
oas_pct = pl.col("#oas") / 100
print(
    df.select(
        "DATE",
        ytw=pl.col("#ytw").round(2),
        oas_bp=pl.col("#oas").round(),
        rates=(pl.col("#ytw") - oas_pct).round(2),
        spread_pct=(100 * oas_pct / pl.col("#ytw")).round(),
    )
)

Output 

shape: (9, 5)
┌────────────┬──────┬────────┬───────┬────────────┐
│ DATE       ┆ ytw  ┆ oas_bp ┆ rates ┆ spread_pct │
│ ---        ┆ ---  ┆ ---    ┆ ---   ┆ ---        │
│ date       ┆ f64  ┆ f64    ┆ f64   ┆ f64        │
╞════════════╪══════╪════════╪═══════╪════════════╡
│ 2026-09-25 ┆ 5.97 ┆ 248.0  ┆ 3.5   ┆ 41.0       │
│ 2026-10-02 ┆ 6.3  ┆ 297.0  ┆ 3.33  ┆ 47.0       │
│ 2026-10-09 ┆ 6.12 ┆ 279.0  ┆ 3.33  ┆ 46.0       │
│ 2026-10-16 ┆ 6.01 ┆ 274.0  ┆ 3.27  ┆ 46.0       │
│ 2026-10-23 ┆ 6.33 ┆ 303.0  ┆ 3.3   ┆ 48.0       │
│ 2026-10-30 ┆ 6.21 ┆ 296.0  ┆ 3.26  ┆ 48.0       │
│ 2026-11-06 ┆ 6.05 ┆ 287.0  ┆ 3.18  ┆ 47.0       │
│ 2026-11-13 ┆ 6.01 ┆ 270.0  ┆ 3.31  ┆ 45.0       │
│ 2026-11-17 ┆ 6.04 ┆ 273.0  ┆ 3.32  ┆ 45.0       │
└────────────┴──────┴────────┴───────┴────────────┘

Watch out

  • Index analytics need universe_type; without it, yield() and spread() return null. PROJECTED is the index as it will be after the next rebalancing, RETURNS the index fixed for this month's returns. Yield to worst accepts only PROJECTED; spreads accept both.
  • per=W gives Friday closes, like weekly BDH data, and the latest close as the last row. frq=W would step back seven days at a time from today.
  • spread(spread_type=OAS) is null for an index. Use OAS_SOVEREIGN, OAS_SWAP, or Z with universe_type.

Notes

  • The same numbers come from BDH: bq.bdh(["I30904EU Index"], ["INDEX_YIELD_TO_WORST", "INDEX_OAS_TSY"], start, end). INDEX_OAS_TSY is the OAS with RETURNS, but in percent instead of basis points.
  • The hedged index H30904EU has the same yield and spread; only its returns differ.

docs.title: Tier 2: spread to call or to maturity
docs.text:
YAS: spread(price=..., workout=...)

The EUR Tier 2 bonds of SEB, Handelsbanken and Swedbank at today's price: Z-spread and yield if the bank calls the bond at the first call date, and if it does not. This is the YAS calculator run from BQL.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
let(#px = px_last();
    #z_call = spread(spread_type=Z, price=#px, workout=TO_NEXT_CALL);
    #z_mat = spread(spread_type=Z, price=#px, workout=TO_MATURITY);
    #y_call = yield(price=#px, workout=TO_NEXT_CALL);
    #y_mat = yield(price=#px, workout=TO_MATURITY);)
get(name, nxt_call_dt, #px, #z_call, #z_mat, #y_call, #y_mat)
for(filter(bondsUniv(ACTIVE, consolidateduplicates=True),
           ticker in ['SEB', 'SHBASS', 'SWEDA'] and crncy() == 'EUR' and
           basel_iii_designation() == 'Tier 2'))
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine(on="ID")
print(
    df.select(
        "name",
        call="nxt_call_dt",
        price=pl.col("#px").round(2),
        z_call=pl.col("#z_call").round(),
        z_mat=pl.col("#z_mat").round(),
        y_call=pl.col("#y_call").round(2),
        y_mat=pl.col("#y_mat").round(2),
        extension=(pl.col("#z_mat") - pl.col("#z_call")).round(),
    ).sort("call")
)

Output 

shape: (9, 8)
┌─────────────────────┬────────────┬────────┬────────┬───────┬────────┬───────┬───────────┐
│ name                ┆ call       ┆ price  ┆ z_call ┆ z_mat ┆ y_call ┆ y_mat ┆ extension │
│ ---                 ┆ ---        ┆ ---    ┆ ---    ┆ ---   ┆ ---    ┆ ---   ┆ ---       │
│ str                 ┆ date       ┆ f64    ┆ f64    ┆ f64   ┆ f64    ┆ f64   ┆ f64       │
╞═════════════════════╪════════════╪════════╪════════╪═══════╪════════╪═══════╪═══════════╡
│ SWEDA 3 ⅝ 08/23/32  ┆ 2027-08-23 ┆ 99.69  ┆ 85.0   ┆ 196.0 ┆ 4.01   ┆ 5.32  ┆ 110.0     │
│ SHBASS 3 ¼ 06/01/33 ┆ 2028-06-01 ┆ 98.69  ┆ 79.0   ┆ 153.0 ┆ 4.14   ┆ 4.91  ┆ 75.0      │
│ SEB 5 08/17/33      ┆ 2028-08-17 ┆ 101.31 ┆ 83.0   ┆ 159.0 ┆ 4.19   ┆ 4.96  ┆ 75.0      │
│ SHBASS 5 08/16/34   ┆ 2029-08-16 ┆ 101.78 ┆ 91.0   ┆ 151.0 ┆ 4.29   ┆ 4.89  ┆ 59.0      │
│ SEB 4 ½ 11/27/34    ┆ 2029-11-27 ┆ 100.92 ┆ 79.0   ┆ 137.0 ┆ 4.17   ┆ 4.76  ┆ 58.0      │
│ SWEDA 3 ½ 08/19/35  ┆ 2030-08-19 ┆ 96.92  ┆ 103.0  ┆ 111.0 ┆ 4.4    ┆ 4.51  ┆ 8.0       │
│ SWEDA 4 ½ 09/29/36  ┆ 2031-09-29 ┆ 99.83  ┆ 117.0  ┆ 113.0 ┆ 4.54   ┆ 4.54  ┆ -4.0      │
│ SHBASS 3 ⅝ 11/04/36 ┆ 2031-11-04 ┆ 96.19  ┆ 113.0  ┆ 125.0 ┆ 4.5    ┆ 4.66  ┆ 12.0      │
│ SEB 4 08/18/37      ┆ 2032-08-18 ┆ 97.48  ┆ 114.0  ┆ 108.0 ┆ 4.51   ┆ 4.5   ┆ -6.0      │
└─────────────────────┴────────────┴────────┴────────┴───────┴────────┴───────┴───────────┘

Watch out

  • price= takes a number or an expression; price=#px runs YAS at px_last(). workout= without price= is rejected with "Incorrect parameters provided".
  • TO_WORST picks the workout with the lower yield, not the lower spread. A bond can be worst to call although its spread to maturity is lower.
  • Without price=, spread() uses Bloomberg's own pricing source, not px_last(). Pass the same price= to every value you compare.

Notes

  • workout= is TO_WORST (the default), TO_NEXT_CALL, TO_NEXT_PUT, TO_MATURITY or TO_CUSTOM. yield() and the other spread types take the same parameters.
  • These bonds reset their coupon to the swap rate plus the original margin if they are not called. extension is the spread to maturity minus the spread to call. When it is positive, the reset margin is above today's market spread and the bank saves money by calling. When it is negative, an investor earns less spread if the bond is not called.

docs.title: One bond at four prices
docs.text:
YAS: workout=TO_CUSTOM, workout_date

The SEB 4 08/18/37 Tier 2 bond, first call 18 August 2032, at four prices: Z-spread to the call, to a custom date two years later, and to maturity, and the yield to worst.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

bond = "DO405623 Corp"  # SEB 4 08/18/37, first call 2032-08-18
rows = []
with BQuery() as bq:
    for price in [96, 98, 100, 102]:
        query = f"""
        get(spread(spread_type=Z, price={price}, workout=TO_NEXT_CALL) as #z_call,
            spread(spread_type=Z, price={price}, workout=TO_CUSTOM,
                   workout_date=2034-08-18) as #z_2034,
            spread(spread_type=Z, price={price}, workout=TO_MATURITY) as #z_mat,
            yield(price={price}, workout=TO_WORST) as #ytw)
        for(['{bond}'])
        """
        rows.append(bq.bql(query).combine().with_columns(price=pl.lit(price)))
print(
    pl.concat(rows).select(
        "price",
        z_call=pl.col("#z_call").round(),
        z_2034=pl.col("#z_2034").round(),
        z_mat=pl.col("#z_mat").round(),
        ytw=pl.col("#ytw").round(2),
    )
)

Output 

shape: (4, 5)
┌───────┬────────┬────────┬───────┬──────┐
│ price ┆ z_call ┆ z_2034 ┆ z_mat ┆ ytw  │
│ ---   ┆ ---    ┆ ---    ┆ ---   ┆ ---  │
│ i32   ┆ f64    ┆ f64    ┆ f64   ┆ f64  │
╞═══════╪════════╪════════╪═══════╪══════╡
│ 96    ┆ 144.0  ┆ 136.0  ┆ 126.0 ┆ 4.68 │
│ 98    ┆ 103.0  ┆ 104.0  ┆ 102.0 ┆ 4.4  │
│ 100   ┆ 63.0   ┆ 73.0   ┆ 78.0  ┆ 4.0  │
│ 102   ┆ 24.0   ┆ 43.0   ┆ 55.0  ┆ 3.61 │
└───────┴────────┴────────┴───────┴──────┘

Notes

  • workout=TO_CUSTOM, workout_date=... assumes the bond is repaid at 100 on that date; workout_price= sets another redemption price. Use it for a call that comes late, or for the date you plan to sell.
  • The spread to the nearest date moves most with the price: the gain or loss against 100 is spread over fewer years.
  • The other direction works too: price(spread=100, spread_type=Z, workout=TO_NEXT_CALL) is the price for a Z-spread of 100 bp to the call, and price(yield=4.5, workout=TO_NEXT_CALL) the price for a yield.

docs.title: SEK AT1 floaters: discount margin
docs.text:
YAS: discount_margin(price=...)

The floating rate AT1s in SEK of six Swedish banks: the quoted margin over STIBOR, the discount margin at today's price, and the discount margin if you pay one point more.

import polars as pl
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

query = """
let(#px = px_last();)
get(name, nxt_call_dt, #px, flt_spread() as #margin,
    discount_margin(price=#px) as #dm,
    discount_margin(price=#px + 1) as #dm_plus_1)
for(filter(bondsUniv(ACTIVE, consolidateduplicates=True),
           ticker in ['SEB', 'SHBASS', 'SBAB', 'LFBANK', 'KLARNA', 'SVEABK'] and
           crncy() == 'SEK' and cpn_typ() == 'FLOATING' and
           basel_iii_designation() == 'Additional Tier 1'))
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bql(query).combine(on="ID")
print(
    df.select(
        "name",
        call="nxt_call_dt",
        price=pl.col("#px").round(2),
        margin="#margin",
        dm=pl.col("#dm").round(),
        dm_plus_1=pl.col("#dm_plus_1").round(),
        bp_per_point=(pl.col("#dm") - pl.col("#dm_plus_1")).round(),
    ).sort("call")
)

Output 

shape: (10, 7)
┌───────────────────┬────────────┬────────┬────────┬───────┬───────────┬──────────────┐

│ ---               ┆ ---        ┆ ---    ┆ ---    ┆ ---   ┆ ---       ┆ ---          │

Notes

  • flt_spread() is the quoted margin, the spread the coupon pays over the reference rate. discount_margin(price=100) is close to it: at par a floater earns its margin.
  • For these perpetual notes the discount margin is to the next call (TO_WORST and TO_NEXT_CALL give the same value). workout=TO_MATURITY changes it.
  • bp_per_point is the discount margin you give up for each point of price. Close to the call date one point costs a lot of margin, so check the call date before you pay up for a short floater.
  • price=#px + 1 shows that price= takes arithmetic too.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
What surprised us while writing these recipes.

Symptom Cause Fix "OAS" numbers match the Z-spread spread() without a type is the Z-spread spread(spread_type=OAS) Each group appears twice after combine(), half of the values null A null group key: capital_contingent_security() is null for most non-CoCos, and combine() does not join null keys if(capital_contingent_security(), true, false) Grouped items over dates do not join, three times as many rows ORIG_IDS is null in every row preferences(dropCols=['ORIG_IDS']) A monthly history on the 17th of each month frq=M steps back from the end date per=M for month-end closes A weekly history on Tuesdays frq=W steps back seven days from today per=W for Friday closes An index's yield or spread is null No universe_type universe_type=PROJECTED (the only one for yield to worst) or RETURNS "Incorrect parameters provided" for spread() or yield() workout= without price= Add price=px_last() or a number The index OAS is 100 times smaller in BDH INDEX_OAS_TSY is in percent, BQL in basis points Multiply the BDH value by 100 The daily average jumps on a holiday Fewer bonds are priced that day Compare the bond count, or use the median Two aliases, one column BQL merges identical expressions, such as spread() and spread(spread_type=Z), into one item Ask for each expression once

Related

See also YAS <GO> and BQLX <GO>. For how bql() and combine() work, see BQL.

docs.title: BDH
docs.text:
Use Case: Retrieve historical data over a date range, such as daily closing prices or volumes.

For weekly and fiscal-year data, holidays, fund flows, CDS indices, FX hedging cost and candles, see the Market History with BDH recipes.

An invalid security has no rows and an invalid field is a column of nulls, with one warning per call that lists them; a range without data, such as a weekend, gives an empty frame that keeps its security, date and field columns, and a request Bloomberg rejects raises BloombergError. 

with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bdh(
        ["TLT US Equity"],
        ["PX_LAST"],
        start_date=date(2019, 1, 1),
        end_date=date(2019, 1, 7),
    )
    print(df)

│ str           ┆ date       ┆ f64     │

│ TLT US Equity ┆ 2019-01-03 ┆ 123.54  │

│ TLT US Equity ┆ 2019-01-07 ┆ 121.75  │

docs.title: BDIB – Bloomberg Data Intraday Bar
docs.text: bdib() fetches pre-aggregated intraday bars directly from Bloomberg, so you can work with 1- to 1440-minute candles without managing tick-level aggregation yourself. Each bar is returned as a row of a Polars DataFrame; its time is the start of the bar, as a naive datetime (no time zone) holding UTC.

docs.title: When to use BDIB
docs.text:
• You need intraday OHLCV bars for a single security over a specific time window.
  • You want Bloomberg to enforce consistent interval lengths (e.g., 5-, 15-, 60-minute bars).

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• start_datetime and end_datetime can be naive or timezone-aware. Naive values are treated as UTC; aware values are converted to UTC before the request is sent. A date means midnight, and an ISO 8601 string ("2024-01-02T08:00:00") is sent as it is.
  • Supported event_type values: TRADE, BID, ASK, BEST_BID, BEST_ASK.
  • Bloomberg enforces the interval range (1-1440 minutes). A request outside that range raises BloombergError with Bloomberg's unspecific message: Response error: Data not available from service. [nid:…] (NOT_AVAILABLE).
  • An unknown security raises BloombergError too (unlike bdp() and bdh(), which give nulls and a warning). A window without bars, for example one older than the few months of intraday history Bloomberg keeps, gives an empty frame that keeps its columns.
  • Optional overrides and options parameters work the same way as in bdp() and bdh()

docs.title: BQL
docs.text:
Use Case: Run more advanced queries to screen securities, calculate analytics (like moving averages), or pull fundamental data with complex conditions.

Returns: The bql() method returns a BqlResult object, which:

  • Acts like a list of Polars DataFrames (one for each item in BQL get statement).
  • Provides a .combine() method to merge DataFrames. With no arguments it preserves the legacy behavior of joining on common columns. Use .combine(on=...) to join only on explicit keys such as "ID" or ["ID", "DATE"].

A query that BQL rejects, for example for a syntax error, does not raise: bql() returns an empty BqlResult, logs the message and keeps it in result.errors; combine() on it raises ValueError with that message. A screen that matches nothing gives the same empty result; its message ("No results match ...") is logged as a warning, not an error.

docs.title: Basic Example
docs.text:
# Fetch the last price of IBM stock
with BQuery() as bq:
    results = bq.bql("get(px_last) for(['IBM US Equity'])")
    print(results[0])  # Access the first DataFrame
Output:

docs.title: Multiple Items - combine()
docs.text:
When querying for multiple items, bql() returns BqlResult object which is actually just a list of polars dataframes with extra method combine() 

# Fetch name and last price of IBM (two items)
with BQuery() as bq:
    results = bq.bql("get(name, px_last) for(['IBM US Equity'])")
Output: 
>>> print(len(results))  # 2 DataFrames
n=2

>>> print(results[0])    # First DataFrame: 'name'
┌───────────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
│ ID            ┆ name                           │
│ ---           ┆ ---                            │
│ str           ┆ str                            │
╞═══════════════╪════════════════════════════════╡
│ IBM US Equity ┆ International Business Machine │
└───────────────┴────────────────────────────────┘

>>> print(results[1])    # Second DataFrame: 'px_last'
┌───────────────┬─────────┬────────────┬──────────┐
│ ID            ┆ px_last ┆ DATE       ┆ CURRENCY │
│ ---           ┆ ---     ┆ ---        ┆ ---      │
│ str           ┆ f64     ┆ date       ┆ str      │
╞═══════════════╪═════════╪════════════╪══════════╡
│ IBM US Equity ┆ 230.82  ┆ 2024-12-14 ┆ USD      │
└───────────────┴─────────┴────────────┴──────────┘

We can use combine() method to join the results into single dataframe: 

>>> combined_df = results.combine(on="ID")
>>> print(combined_df)
Output: 
┌───────────────┬────────────────────────────────┬─────────┬────────────┬──────────┐
│ ID            ┆ name                           ┆ px_last ┆ DATE       ┆ CURRENCY │
│ ---           ┆ ---                            ┆ ---     ┆ ---        ┆ ---      │
│ str           ┆ str                            ┆ f64     ┆ date       ┆ str      │
╞═══════════════╪════════════════════════════════╪═════════╪════════════╪══════════╡
│ IBM US Equity ┆ International Business Machine ┆ 230.82  ┆ 2024-12-14 ┆ USD      │
└───────────────┴────────────────────────────────┴─────────┴────────────┴──────────┘

By default, combine() keeps the historical behavior and joins each result DataFrame on all common column names. This is convenient for simple BQL results, but it can be too broad when several item tables share metadata columns such as DATE, CURRENCY, PERIOD, VALUE, or MULTIPLIER.

A row whose shared columns hold nulls matches nothing and appears twice, once from each side: for example a security for which BQL has no DATE.

with BQuery() as bq:
    results = bq.bql(
        "get(px_last, px_volume) for(['IBM US Equity', 'NOT A SECURITY Equity'])"
    )

>>> print(results.combine())  # joins on ID and DATE
shape: (3, 5)
┌───────────────────────┬─────────┬────────────┬──────────┬───────────┐
│ ID                    ┆ px_last ┆ DATE       ┆ CURRENCY ┆ px_volume │
│ ---                   ┆ ---     ┆ ---        ┆ ---      ┆ ---       │
│ str                   ┆ f64     ┆ date       ┆ str      ┆ f64       │
╞═══════════════════════╪═════════╪════════════╪══════════╪═══════════╡
│ IBM US Equity         ┆ 247.13  ┆ 2026-11-16 ┆ USD      ┆ 4750.0    │
│ NOT A SECURITY Equity ┆ null    ┆ null       ┆ null     ┆ null      │
│ NOT A SECURITY Equity ┆ null    ┆ null       ┆ null     ┆ null      │
└───────────────────────┴─────────┴────────────┴──────────┴───────────┘

>>> print(results.combine(on="ID"))  # one row per security
shape: (2, 6)
┌───────────────────────┬─────────┬────────────┬──────────┬───────────┬────────────────┐
│ ID                    ┆ px_last ┆ DATE       ┆ CURRENCY ┆ px_volume ┆ DATE_px_volume │
│ ---                   ┆ ---     ┆ ---        ┆ ---      ┆ ---       ┆ ---            │
│ str                   ┆ f64     ┆ date       ┆ str      ┆ f64       ┆ date           │
╞═══════════════════════╪═════════╪════════════╪══════════╪═══════════╪════════════════╡
│ IBM US Equity         ┆ 247.13  ┆ 2026-11-16 ┆ USD      ┆ 4750.0    ┆ 2026-11-16     │
│ NOT A SECURITY Equity ┆ null    ┆ null       ┆ null     ┆ null      ┆ null           │
└───────────────────────┴─────────┴────────────┴──────────┴───────────┴────────────────┘

For safer joins, pass the intended key columns explicitly; combine(on="ID") gives one row per security:

# Join only by security ID. Other common columns are kept as data columns.
combined_df = results.combine(on="ID")

# Join by a compound key when both columns are true row identifiers.
combined_df = results.combine(on=["ID", "DATE"])

# Use Polars join names. "full" is the default for explicit joins.
combined_df = results.combine(on="ID", how="inner")

If non-key columns overlap when using on=..., they are preserved with suffixes based on the BQL item name, for example DATE_#ret_1d. To fail instead of suffixing overlapping non-key columns, use:

combined_df = results.combine(on="ID", allow_common_columns=False)

docs.title: Screening
docs.text:
Example of using saved SRCH search and filtering on ticker: Find list of SEB and Handelsbanken's AT1 bonds and print their names, duration and Z-Spread. The result of the query is list of 3 polars dataframes and can be conveniently combined using combine() method. 

query = """
    let(#dur=duration(duration_type=MODIFIED); 
        #zsprd=spread(spread_type=Z);) 
    get(name(), #dur, #zsprd) 
    for(filter(screenresults(type=SRCH, screen_name='@COCO'), 
            ticker in ['SEB', 'SHBASS']))
"""

with BQuery() as bq:
    results = bq.bql(query)
    combined_df = results.combine(on="ID")
    print(combined_df)

docs.text:
Get current axes of all Swedish USD AT1 bonds. More axes queries (per dealer, large axes, net axes, the last 1 and 5 weeks) are in the Dealer Axes recipes. 

# Get current axes for Swedish AT1 bonds in USD
query="""
    let(#ax=axes();)
    get(security_des, #ax)
    for(filter(bondsuniv(ACTIVE),
        crncy()=='USD' and
        basel_iii_designation() == 'Additional Tier 1' and
        country_iso() == 'SE'))
"""

with BQuery() as bq:
    results = bq.bql(query)

docs.title: Segments
docs.text:
The following example shows handling of two data-items with different length. The first dataframe describes the segments (and has length 5 in this case), while the second dataframe contains time series. One can join the dataframes on common columns and pivot the segments into columns as shown below: 

# revenue per segment
query = """
    let(#segment=segment_name();
        #revenue=sales_Rev_turn(fpt=q, fpr=range(2023Q3, 2024Q3));
        )
    get(#segment, #revenue)
    for(segments('GTN US Equity',type=reported,hierarchy=PRODUCT, level=1))
"""
with BQuery() as bq:
    results = bq.bql(query)
    df = results.combine().pivot(
        index="PERIOD_END_DATE", on="#segment", values="#revenue"
    )
    print(df)
Output:

docs.title: BSRCH
docs.text:
Use case: Excel-style searches (SRCH/BI domains). Good for running saved SRCH screens or Bloomberg BI templates.

A failed search raises BloombergError (a ValueError), and a search without results gives an empty frame that keeps its columns.

Key points: - Column types follow what Bloomberg sends (StringValue or DoubleValue): a number sent as text stays a string, and a blank cell in a numeric column becomes null. - Pass overrides as a dict or as (name, value) pairs; values are stringified. Common keys: LIMIT to raise the row cap (default ~5k), custom keys like BIKEY for BI templates, or domain-specific parameters.

docs.title: Example: two COCO bonds (LIMIT=2)
docs.text:
from polars_bloomberg import BQuery

with BQuery() as bq:
    df = bq.bsrch("FI:SRCHEX.@COCO", overrides={"LIMIT": 2})
    print(df)

# shape: (2, 1)
